# Proposal: Deploying an Internal AI Assistant Across the Organization

## Background

Employees across the organization spend significant time searching for information, drafting and reviewing content, summarizing meetings, and navigating internal processes. Knowledge is distributed across collaboration tools, document repositories, policies, and business systems, making it difficult to find reliable answers quickly. A secure internal AI assistant can reduce this friction by helping employees work with approved organizational information through a familiar, conversational interface.

This proposal recommends a phased deployment of an internal AI assistant for the organization’s 5,000 employees. The assistant will help with common knowledge and productivity tasks while respecting existing access permissions and security controls. It will be introduced as a governed workplace capability—not as a replacement for professional judgment, business systems, or employee roles.

## Objectives

The deployment will make trusted organizational knowledge easier to find and use, reduce time spent on routine information and content tasks, and provide a consistent employee experience across departments. It will also establish the governance, technical controls, and operating practices needed to expand AI use responsibly over time.

By the end of the initial rollout, employees should be able to use the assistant to locate and summarize approved internal content, draft and refine common workplace materials, and receive answers that cite their sources where available. The organization should also have a clear process for reviewing performance, addressing risks, incorporating employee feedback, and deciding which additional capabilities are appropriate.

## Scope

The initial release will provide a web-based assistant accessible through the organization’s approved collaboration environment. It will support tasks such as answering questions from selected internal policies and guidance, summarizing documents, drafting routine communications, and helping employees locate relevant procedures and resources. Responses based on internal content will include links or citations to source material when technically available, so employees can verify important information.

The first release will connect only to a defined set of approved knowledge sources, such as selected policy libraries, employee guidance, and operational documentation. Access to connected content will follow existing permissions; the assistant will not make restricted information available to users who could not otherwise access it. The deployment will use approved AI services and enterprise security controls, including identity management, encryption, logging, retention rules, and administrative oversight.

The assistant will not make employment, financial, legal, safety, or other high-impact decisions. It will not autonomously take actions in business systems or provide unrestricted access to sensitive records. Any future expansion into additional data sources, workflows, or higher-impact use cases will require a separate privacy, security, legal, and business review.

## Delivery approach and timeline

The project is expected to take approximately nine months from approval to organization-wide availability. The first month will establish executive sponsorship, confirm priority use cases, appoint governance owners, and agree on baseline measures. During this period, the team will also assess candidate platforms, data sources, integration requirements, and applicable security and privacy obligations.

Months two and three will focus on solution design and preparation. The project team will select the approved platform, define the assistant’s boundaries and user experience, configure identity and access controls, and prepare the initial knowledge sources. Content owners will review the materials selected for launch to identify outdated, duplicated, or unsuitable content. The team will establish evaluation procedures for answer quality, source attribution, security behavior, and user experience before employees are invited to use the system.

A controlled pilot will run during months four and five with approximately 300–500 employees representing a range of roles, departments, and technical confidence levels. Pilot participants will receive short training and clear guidance on appropriate use. The project team will monitor adoption, task completion, answer quality, user feedback, and reported issues. Findings will be used to improve the assistant, update content, and resolve operational or governance gaps before expansion.

Months six and seven will support a staged rollout to the remaining workforce, using department-based waves and targeted communications. Training will be available through brief online materials, manager guidance, and drop-in support. The final two months will focus on stabilization, measurement, issue resolution, and handover to the permanent service owners. At the end of the initial deployment, leadership will review results and approve, adjust, or defer further expansion.

## Resource requirements

The work will require an executive sponsor and a cross-functional delivery team with authority to coordinate technology, information, and business owners. For the nine-month implementation, the organization should plan for approximately 8–12 full-time-equivalent staff, with some roles assigned part-time. Core participation will include a product or program lead, AI and platform engineers, data and integration specialists, information security and privacy representatives, legal or compliance support, user-experience and accessibility expertise, content owners, change and communications staff, and service-desk support.

Department leaders and subject-matter experts will need to contribute time to prioritize use cases, review content, validate answers, and support local adoption. The organization should also designate permanent owners for the assistant’s product roadmap, technical operations, content quality, governance, and employee support before the pilot begins.

Funding will be required for the AI platform and associated usage, integration and testing, security and monitoring capabilities, content preparation, training, and ongoing support. The project team should establish a detailed cost estimate during the first month, based on platform pricing, expected usage, existing infrastructure, and the final set of integrations. The estimate should distinguish one-time implementation costs from recurring service costs and include capacity for ongoing evaluation and improvement.

## Governance and risk management

A cross-functional governance group will oversee the assistant throughout the project and after launch. It will include representatives from technology, security, privacy, legal or compliance, human resources, records management, and the business. The group will approve use cases and data sources, review evaluation results, set retention and monitoring rules, and determine how incidents and employee concerns are handled.

Employees will be told what the assistant can and cannot do, what information they should not enter, and how to verify important answers. The service will be tested for reliability, inappropriate disclosure, harmful or misleading outputs, accessibility, and consistency across representative user groups. A clear feedback and reporting channel will allow employees to flag incorrect answers, unsafe behavior, or content problems. Material changes to the model, data sources, or capabilities will be reviewed before release.

## Success criteria

The deployment will be considered successful if it demonstrates useful, safe, and sustained adoption—not simply account activation. By the end of the first six months after general availability, the project will target at least 60% monthly active use among employees, with at least 70% of surveyed users reporting that the assistant helps them complete selected tasks more efficiently. In pilot and post-launch testing, the assistant should provide a relevant, source-supported answer for at least 80% of questions drawn from the approved knowledge set, while respecting access permissions in all tested scenarios.

The organization will also measure changes in time spent locating information and completing selected routine tasks, aiming for a median time reduction of at least 20% in the use cases chosen for evaluation. Service reliability should meet the organization’s agreed availability target, and support requests, user satisfaction, and unresolved quality issues should remain within thresholds set before the pilot. Security or privacy incidents attributable to the assistant must be investigated and managed under established response procedures, with no unresolved critical issues at the point of wider rollout.

Results will be reviewed against baseline measures established before the pilot. The governance group will recommend whether to continue, modify, or expand the service based on these measures, employee feedback, operational cost, and risk. This approach gives the organization a practical path to deliver immediate productivity benefits while building the controls and experience needed for responsible long-term use of AI.

# Project Proposal: Enterprise Internal AI Assistant

## Background

Employees across the organization spend significant time searching for information, drafting and summarizing content, and navigating internal processes. Relevant knowledge is often spread across collaboration tools, document repositories, and business systems, making it difficult to find reliable answers quickly. A secure internal AI assistant can reduce this friction by giving employees a consistent way to discover approved information and complete routine knowledge-work tasks.

This proposal establishes a governed assistant for a 5,000-employee organization. The assistant will use approved enterprise AI services and provide answers grounded in authorized internal content. It will complement—not replace—existing systems and human expertise. Its responses will be presented as assistance, with citations or links to source material where available.

## Objectives

The project will make trusted organizational knowledge easier to access, reduce time spent on routine drafting and summarization, and improve the consistency of employee support. It will also establish the security, governance, and measurement practices required to use generative AI responsibly at scale.

The initial deployment will prioritize practical, low-risk employee use cases. These include finding and summarizing internal policies and procedures, answering questions from approved knowledge bases, summarizing documents or meetings, and drafting or revising common business communications. The project will create a foundation for future workflow integrations, subject to separate risk review and approval.

## Scope

The deployment will provide access to an internal assistant for all 5,000 employees, with an initial pilot group followed by staged organization-wide availability. The assistant will be accessible through an approved web interface and, where feasible, the organization’s primary collaboration platform. Access will use existing identity and access controls, and content retrieval will respect the permissions already assigned to each user.

The first release will connect to a limited set of high-value, well-maintained knowledge sources, such as approved policies, employee guidance, and selected operational documentation. Content owners will be responsible for confirming that material is current and appropriate for use. Responses based on internal sources will link back to those sources wherever possible, and the interface will clearly communicate that AI-generated content may be incomplete or incorrect.

The project will not authorize the assistant to make employment, legal, financial, safety, or other high-impact decisions; approve transactions; or take actions in business systems without human review. It will not ingest sensitive repositories by default. Any expansion to new data sources, user groups, or automated actions will require security, privacy, legal, and business-owner review.

## Delivery Timeline

The project is planned for approximately six months from approval to organization-wide release. During the first four weeks, the team will confirm priority use cases, select the technical approach, inventory candidate data sources, complete privacy and security assessments, and define baseline measures. The following six weeks will be used to configure the assistant, establish identity and access controls, connect the first approved knowledge sources, and create evaluation and support processes.

A four-week pilot will then involve approximately 200–300 employees drawn from representative functions and technical skill levels. The pilot will assess answer quality, source reliability, usability, accessibility, and employee trust. Findings will be used to remediate issues and refine training and guidance. In the next four weeks, the assistant will be released to successive employee cohorts, supported by communications, training, and service-desk readiness. The final two weeks will focus on stabilization, performance review, and transition to ongoing operations. Timing may be adjusted if data readiness or security findings require additional remediation.

## Resource Requirements

The project will require a cross-functional team of approximately 10–14 full-time-equivalent staff during design and rollout. Core roles include a product lead, project manager, AI or solution architect, two to three engineers, one or two data and integration specialists, a security and privacy lead, a testing and evaluation lead, a change-management and communications lead, and service-desk representatives. Legal, HR, records management, accessibility, and business data owners will contribute part-time review and approval.

The organization will also need an approved AI platform, identity integration, secure hosting and monitoring, and the necessary model and usage capacity for a 5,000-person audience. Costs will depend on the selected platform, existing enterprise agreements, usage volumes, and the number of data integrations. Before procurement or expansion, Finance and IT should validate a total-cost estimate that includes licensing, implementation, support, monitoring, and ongoing model usage.

After launch, a standing operations group of approximately 4–6 FTE should manage product improvements, integrations, quality monitoring, access and incident processes, user support, and governance. Departmental content owners will remain responsible for the accuracy and maintenance of their source material.

## Success Criteria

The project will be considered successful if it delivers secure access to the assistant for all 5,000 employees, with no unresolved critical security or privacy findings at organization-wide release. During the pilot, at least 80% of evaluated responses to approved knowledge questions should be judged useful and adequately grounded in permitted sources, with a clear process for correcting failures and removing unsuitable content.

Within six months of organization-wide release, the target is for at least 60% of employees to have tried the assistant and at least 35% to use it monthly. User surveys should show improved ease of finding internal information and an average usefulness rating of at least 4 out of 5 among regular users. For the selected use cases, the organization should demonstrate a measurable reduction in time spent on information retrieval or routine drafting, using pilot and post-launch measurements against an established baseline.

The team will review usage, answer quality, user feedback, incidents, and support demand monthly. Continued investment and any expansion beyond the initial scope will be based on these results, compliance with governance requirements, and demonstrated value to employees and the organization.

Departmental champions and content owners will provide additional part-time support to keep source material accurate and identify emerging needs.

The budget should cover platform licensing or consumption, implementation and integration work, security testing, content preparation, training and communications, support operations, and ongoing monitoring. A detailed cost estimate will be prepared during the first month after platform options, usage assumptions, and integration requirements are confirmed.

## Governance and Risk Management

An executive sponsor will be accountable for the program, supported by a cross-functional AI governance group with representation from technology, security, privacy, legal, HR, records management, and business operations. The group will approve use cases, review material changes, monitor incidents and emerging risks, and ensure that employees understand appropriate use.

The assistant will identify itself as AI-generated, explain relevant limitations, and encourage users to verify important information against cited sources. The organization will provide clear guidance on prohibited or restricted data, appropriate review of outputs, and the reporting of inaccurate or harmful responses. Logs and usage data will be collected only as permitted by policy and applicable law, with transparent retention and access rules. A documented incident process will support prompt investigation, containment, and remediation.

## Success Criteria

The project will be considered successful when the assistant is available to all 5,000 employees and at least 60 percent of employees have used it during the preceding 30 days by the end of the first year. At least 70 percent of surveyed active users should report that it helps them complete relevant tasks more efficiently, and pilot measurement should show a median time saving of at least 20 percent on selected routine tasks compared with baseline.

For internal knowledge questions, at least 80 percent of sampled responses should be rated useful and sufficiently accurate by reviewers, with source attribution provided for at least 90 percent of responses that rely on internal content. The service must pass security and privacy review, enforce source permissions in testing, and have no unresolved critical findings at launch. The project will also track support demand, user satisfaction, usage across departments, accessibility issues, operating cost, and reported incidents.

Results will be reviewed at the end of the pilot, at organization-wide launch, and quarterly during the first year. If adoption, quality, or safety measures fall below agreed thresholds, expansion will pause while the team addresses the underlying issues.

Someone needs a machine that can run one legacy app nobody has documented since 2019. A regional office has a lease that ends three months later than the rest. The “standard” dock turns out not to fit under half the desks, and the person who knows why is on vacation until Thursday. None of these problems is large enough to stop the project. Together, they become the project.

So you learn to treat the spreadsheet as a hypothesis, not a plan. Keep a small pool of oddball machines, give the support team a say before the order goes in, and leave enough slack in the schedule for reality to arrive in batches. The refresh still happens. It just stops pretending that every device belongs to the same story.

A department has a specialist application that only runs on the old image. Someone’s laptop is “mission critical” in a way that is not documented anywhere, but is apparently known to three people who are all on leave. The new docks arrive with the wrong cables, the right cables arrive without the docks, and a device that passed every test in the lab refuses to join the network in one particular meeting room.

By then, the schedule is less a plan than a theory about how people might behave. You start tracking the work that never made it into the spreadsheet: backing up local files, finding owners for orphaned equipment, explaining why “same model” does not mean “same setup.” The refresh still gets done. It just turns out the real unit of work was never the laptop. It was every small dependency everyone had stopped noticing.

Someone needs a machine that runs a piece of software last updated when the building still had a fax machine. Someone else has a dock that works only if you plug it in before the laptop, which nobody knew because the person who knew left in March. The tidy categories in the spreadsheet begin to blur: standard, special case, special case of a special case.

The work shifts from ordering devices to finding out how people actually use them. You start asking for photos of desks, lists of peripherals, and the name of the one application nobody wants to mention until migration day. The refresh still happens, eventually. It just stops being a hardware project and becomes a tour of every assumption the organization made about its own workflows.

A machine that cannot run the approved image. A team that needs a specialist tool nobody remembered to inventory. A laptop that was supposed to be retired but is still attached to a process no one wants to interrupt. None of these are hard problems individually. The trouble is that each one arrives with its own owner, deadline, and definition of “temporary,” and suddenly the refresh plan is less a schedule than a negotiation.

So the useful work happens before the boxes show up: finding the people who know where the dependencies are buried, deciding which exceptions deserve a real path and which just need a firm end date, and making sure support can tell the difference between a new device and a new problem. The rollout still matters. It just turns out that replacing the hardware is the part you can put on a spreadsheet.

# Project Proposal: Enterprise AI Assistant Deployment

## Background

A 5,000-employee organization holds valuable operational knowledge across policies, procedures, project materials, and other approved internal sources. Employees often spend significant time finding that information, synthesizing documents, and completing routine writing and analysis. An internal AI assistant can make this knowledge easier to use while giving employees a consistent, secure way to apply generative AI to everyday work.

This proposal recommends deploying a secure, organization-wide assistant that answers questions using approved internal content and supports common tasks such as summarizing, drafting, and synthesizing information. The assistant will operate within the organization’s existing identity, security, privacy, and records-management controls. It will support employees’ work, not make consequential decisions or replace accountable human judgment.

## Objectives

The project will provide employees with a simple, trusted way to find and use approved organizational knowledge. It will aim to reduce time spent searching for information and completing routine knowledge work, improve consistency in how internal guidance is applied, and establish a governed foundation for future AI capabilities.

The deployment will also create a repeatable process for evaluating AI quality, managing content and access, responding to issues, and incorporating employee feedback. Success will depend not only on launching the technology, but on ensuring that employees understand its appropriate uses and can recognize when an answer needs verification.

## Scope

The initial release will be available to employees through an authenticated web interface, with integration into existing collaboration tools considered where it can be delivered without compromising security or delaying the core launch. The assistant will use retrieval-augmented generation to answer questions from a defined set of approved internal sources. Responses will cite their source material wherever possible, and users will be able to report inaccurate, incomplete, or inappropriate answers.

Initial capabilities will include searching and summarizing approved internal documents; answering questions about policies, procedures, and organizational guidance; drafting and revising common workplace content; and synthesizing material supplied by the user. Access to source content will respect existing permissions. The assistant will not expose material a user is not authorized to access.

The first release will exclude autonomous actions such as sending communications, changing records, or approving requests. It will not make employment, legal, financial, medical, or other high-impact decisions, and it will not be presented as a substitute for professional advice or authoritative policy interpretation. Unapproved or highly sensitive information will not be indexed until the relevant data owners, privacy, security, and legal teams have approved its use.

## Delivery approach and timeline

The project is expected to take approximately 24 weeks from approval to organization-wide launch, followed by a 90-day period of adoption and performance measurement. The schedule assumes timely access to selected content sources, executive sponsorship, and availability of subject-matter experts.

During weeks 1–4, the project team will confirm priority use cases, select the initial content sources, document data classifications and access requirements, and establish governance, evaluation, and support processes. This phase will conclude with approval of the solution architecture, security and privacy controls, pilot plan, and baseline measures for employee effort and satisfaction.

During weeks 5–10, the team will configure the assistant, integrate identity and access controls, connect the approved content sources, and build the initial experience. It will also develop a representative evaluation set, test answer quality and citations, conduct security and privacy reviews, and prepare employee guidance and support materials. A launch decision will depend on meeting agreed quality and risk thresholds.

During weeks 11–14, the assistant will be piloted with approximately 500 employees across a range of roles and business areas. The project team will monitor answer quality, access behavior, usability, support requests, and employee feedback. It will correct priority issues and confirm that the service can operate reliably before expanding access.

During weeks 15–20, access will expand in planned waves to approximately 1,500 employees and then to the remaining workforce. Communications, training, and manager guidance will accompany each wave. The final four weeks will focus on stabilization, targeted adoption support, and handover to the ongoing service team. The 90-day post-launch review will assess usage, employee outcomes, quality, safety, and the case for further investment.

## Governance, security, and operations

A cross-functional steering group will provide oversight, resolve issues, and approve material changes to scope or risk. It should include executive sponsorship and representation from technology, information security, privacy, legal, records management, human resources, communications, and the business areas whose content is included.

The service will use enterprise authentication, role-based access, encryption in transit and at rest, and appropriate logging and retention controls. Before launch, the organization will confirm how prompts and responses are handled by the chosen platform, including whether they may be used to train external models. Content owners will approve sources for indexing and remain responsible for their accuracy and currency. A defined process will cover incident response, user feedback, content corrections, model or configuration changes, and periodic access and quality reviews.

Employees will receive concise guidance on suitable uses, data-handling expectations, verification of AI-generated content, and how to report a problem. Training will emphasize that the assistant can be useful without being infallible: employees remain responsible for checking important outputs and following established approval processes.

## Resource requirements

Delivery will require a dedicated core team of approximately eight to ten full-time-equivalent staff over the main implementation period. The team should include a product or program lead, solution architect, AI or machine-learning engineers, data and integration engineers, a security specialist, a user-experience or service designer, a change and communications lead, and a test and evaluation lead. Some roles may be supplied by existing teams or contracted specialists, provided that ownership and decision-making responsibilities are clear.

Part-time contributions will also be needed from privacy, legal, records-management, identity and platform operations, help desk, and business subject-matter experts. Content owners will need to identify authoritative sources, confirm permissions, resolve content-quality issues, and participate in evaluation. Managers and local champions will support employee communications and adoption.

The organization will need an approved AI platform and the associated hosting, licensing, and usage capacity; secure integrations with identity and selected content repositories; monitoring and evaluation tooling; and a support channel for questions and incident reporting. Platform and consumption costs should be confirmed during the first phase, once the deployment model, expected usage, and data requirements have been validated. Funding should also cover employee training, accessibility testing, security assessment, and post-launch service ownership.

## Success criteria

The project will be considered ready for organization-wide launch when security, privacy, access-control, and operational reviews are complete; priority content sources are approved; and the assistant meets the agreed quality and reliability thresholds on a representative evaluation set. As a proposed threshold, at least 90 percent of reviewed answers to in-scope questions should be rated accurate and useful, with citations supporting source-based answers and no unresolved critical security or privacy findings.

At 90 days after full launch, success will be assessed against the following targets: at least 60 percent of employees use the assistant monthly; at least 80 percent of employees complete or receive the required usage guidance; and a representative survey shows that at least 70 percent of active users find the assistant useful for their work. For selected, measurable tasks, user research should demonstrate a reduction of at least 25 percent in time spent finding information or producing a first draft compared with the pre-launch baseline.

The organization will also track answer-quality ratings, citation coverage, failed or unanswered questions, reported issues, service availability, and support demand. The target is no confirmed material data-access or privacy incident attributable to the assistant, with all reported high-severity issues triaged under the established incident process. Results will be reviewed by the steering group after the first 90 days to decide whether to expand source coverage, add integrations, adjust controls, or refine the service.

## Recommendation

Approve a 24-week deployment program, beginning with a four-week discovery and governance phase, and appoint an executive sponsor and cross-functional steering group. This approach will deliver useful capability to employees while making security, content quality, employee readiness, and measurable outcomes prerequisites for scale.

# Proposal: Deployment of an Internal AI Assistant

## Background

Employees across a 5,000-person organization spend significant time searching for information, navigating policies and procedures, and drafting or summarizing routine content. Relevant knowledge is often spread across collaboration platforms, document repositories, intranet pages, and business systems. An internal AI assistant can make approved organizational knowledge easier to find and use, while helping employees complete common writing and information tasks more efficiently.

The assistant will be deployed as a secure, organization-wide service rather than as a standalone public chatbot. It will use approved enterprise AI services, respect existing access permissions, and provide links or citations to the source material behind its answers. Its purpose will be to assist employees—not to make consequential decisions, replace expert review, or act autonomously in business systems.

## Objectives

The project will establish a trusted, accessible AI assistant for all employees and demonstrate measurable improvements in how they find, understand, and work with organizational information. The assistant will answer questions grounded in approved internal content, summarize and draft routine documents, and help employees locate relevant policies, processes, and resources.

The deployment will also create durable capabilities for managing AI safely: clear ownership, security and privacy controls, content-quality practices, employee guidance, and a process for evaluating and improving the service. By launching in stages, the organization can test usefulness and safeguards with representative employees before expanding access.

## Scope

The initial release will be available to all 5,000 employees through an approved web interface, with single sign-on and support for desktop and mobile access where the selected platform permits. It will connect to a prioritized set of authoritative knowledge sources, such as the intranet, policy library, and selected document repositories. Integration will be limited to sources that can be permissioned, monitored, and maintained appropriately.

The assistant will support knowledge retrieval with source citations, summarization, rewriting, drafting, and other low-risk productivity tasks. It will provide clear notices when it is uncertain or lacks a reliable source, and users will be able to give feedback on responses. Access to content will follow existing identity and permissions controls; the assistant will not expose material a user could not otherwise access.

The first release will not make employment, financial, legal, health, or other high-impact decisions; provide unreviewed professional advice; or execute transactions and changes in business systems. Any future expansion into those areas will require separate risk assessment, governance approval, and testing. The service will be governed by documented rules for acceptable use, data retention, incident response, and human review.

## Delivery approach and timeline

The project is expected to take approximately 24 weeks from approval to full deployment. During weeks one through four, the team will confirm business priorities, select the platform and technical approach, identify authoritative content sources, establish governance, and document security, privacy, and legal requirements. It will also define baseline measures for current information-search effort and employee experience.

During weeks five through ten, the team will configure the assistant, connect the first content sources, implement identity and permission controls, and establish logging, monitoring, and feedback processes. Content owners will review the material selected for launch, while security and privacy teams test the design and controls.

A controlled pilot will run during weeks eleven through fourteen with approximately 300 to 500 employees drawn from different functions, locations, and levels of digital experience. Pilot testing will assess answer quality, citation accuracy, usability, accessibility, response times, and safety. The team will address material issues before expanding access.

During weeks fifteen through twenty, access will expand in waves to approximately 1,000 employees and then to the rest of the organization, subject to agreed readiness criteria. Communications, brief training, and role-specific guidance will accompany each wave. Weeks twenty-one through twenty-four will focus on stabilization, support, performance review, and prioritizing improvements for the next release.

## Resource requirements

The project will require a cross-functional core team averaging approximately eight to ten full-time-equivalent staff during delivery. This team should include a product lead, project manager, AI or solution architect, software and integration engineers, data or knowledge specialists, security and privacy representatives, a user-experience designer, a change and communications lead, and testing and evaluation support. Legal, accessibility, records-management, procurement, and business subject-matter experts will contribute part-time as needed.

Business units will appoint content owners to identify authoritative sources, resolve outdated or conflicting material, and approve content for use. A network of employee champions will support the pilot and rollout. After launch, the organization should retain a smaller ongoing service team responsible for product ownership, platform operations, content quality, user support, and periodic safety reviews.

Funding will be needed for the AI platform and hosting, integration and monitoring tools, implementation support where required, employee communications and training, and ongoing service operations. Final cost estimates should be confirmed during the first four weeks, once the platform, usage assumptions, data sources, and service-level requirements are established.

## Success criteria

The project will be considered successful when the assistant is available to all 5,000 employees, operates within approved security and privacy controls, and has clear ownership and support arrangements. Before general release, testing should show that at least 90 percent of answers to a representative set of approved knowledge questions are factually acceptable and correctly grounded in cited sources. Permission testing must confirm that the assistant does not reveal restricted content to unauthorized users, and any critical security or safety findings must be resolved before expansion.

Within three months of full rollout, the target is for at least 60 percent of employees to have tried the assistant and at least 35 percent to be monthly active users. Employee surveys should show improved ease of finding internal information, with a target of a 20 percent reduction in reported time spent on common knowledge-search tasks among regular users. At least 75 percent of surveyed users should rate responses to supported tasks as useful, while support requests, negative feedback, and quality evaluations should be reviewed regularly and lead to documented improvements.

Success will be assessed against a baseline established before the pilot. Adoption alone will not be treated as proof of value: the organization will also track answer quality, user confidence, time saved, accessibility, incidents, and the freshness of connected content. Results will be reviewed at the end of the pilot and again three months after full deployment to determine whether to expand the assistant’s capabilities, refine its content coverage, or adjust its operating model.

# Project Proposal: Enterprise Internal AI Assistant

## Background

Employees across the organization spend significant time searching for information, interpreting internal policies, and repeating routine knowledge-work tasks. Relevant material is often spread across document repositories, the intranet, and service systems, making it difficult to find a reliable answer quickly. A secure internal AI assistant would provide a single, conversational way to access approved organizational knowledge and assist with common work tasks.

This proposal recommends deploying an enterprise AI assistant for all 5,000 employees. The assistant will draw on approved internal sources, respect existing access permissions, and provide citations so employees can verify its answers. It will be introduced in phases, with security, privacy, accuracy, and responsible use built into the design and rollout.

## Objectives

The project will make trusted internal information easier to find and use, reduce time spent on routine search and drafting tasks, and improve the consistency of responses to common employee questions. It will give employees a simple, supported way to use AI at work while establishing clear standards for data handling, human review, and acceptable use.

The assistant will be evaluated on measurable business outcomes as well as adoption and safety. Success will mean that employees use it regularly, report meaningful time savings, can verify its answers against authoritative sources, and can do so without compromising confidential information or existing access controls.

## Scope

The project will deliver an employee-facing assistant accessible through the organization’s approved digital workplace, with single sign-on and support for desktop and mobile use where available. Initial knowledge sources will include approved policies, procedures, frequently asked questions, and selected internal document repositories. Integrations will be prioritized according to business value, technical readiness, and data-owner approval; likely early candidates include the intranet, document management system, and HR or IT knowledge bases.

The assistant will answer questions using retrieved internal content, identify its sources, and indicate when it lacks sufficient information. It may also support low-risk tasks such as summarizing approved documents and drafting routine communications. Responses will remain subject to employee review. The initial release will not make employment, financial, legal, or other consequential decisions; act autonomously on behalf of employees; or access sensitive data sources without explicit security, privacy, and business-owner approval.

The project includes platform and integration design, data preparation, security and privacy assessment, model and answer-quality evaluation, user testing, training, communications, and post-launch support. It does not include replacing existing systems of record, granting new access to restricted information, or training a general-purpose model on confidential organizational data.

## Delivery approach and timeline

The project is planned as a 24-week delivery, followed by a 90-day period of measured operation and improvement. During weeks 1–4, the project team will confirm priority use cases, identify source systems and data owners, establish baseline measures, and complete the architecture, privacy, security, and governance reviews. This phase will also define acceptable-use guidance and the criteria for approving content sources.

During weeks 5–8, the team will configure the assistant platform, establish identity and permission controls, connect the first approved content sources, and build the initial user experience. It will create evaluation sets from representative employee questions and test retrieval, citations, accuracy, and refusal behavior. High-risk data and actions will remain excluded unless specifically approved.

During weeks 9–12, a representative pilot group of approximately 300–500 employees will test the assistant across a range of roles and work patterns. The team will monitor answer quality, usability, latency, access-control behavior, and user feedback. Pilot findings will inform refinements to content, prompts, training, and support procedures. Expansion will proceed only when agreed security and quality gates are met.

During weeks 13–20, access will expand in successive waves to the full employee population, with brief training, communications, and support available at each stage. The rollout will prioritize high-value teams and source systems while maintaining a clear route for reporting incorrect answers or suspected data exposure. Weeks 21–24 will focus on stabilization, resolving adoption barriers, improving priority content, and transferring routine operations to the designated service team.

For the first 90 days after broad launch, the project will continue to review usage, quality, safety, and employee feedback. The team will make controlled improvements and recommend which additional use cases or data sources should be considered next.

## Resource requirements

The project requires a cross-functional core team of approximately 12–16 full-time equivalents during delivery. This should include an executive sponsor and a dedicated product owner; a program manager; two to four AI, application, and platform engineers; two to three data and integration specialists; one or two security, privacy, and risk specialists; a quality and evaluation lead with testing support; and one or two specialists in user experience, communications, and change management. HR, IT, legal, records management, and business data owners will provide part-time subject-matter expertise and approve content within their areas.

After launch, the organization should plan for a continuing operational team of approximately 3–5 full-time equivalents, covering product management, platform and integration maintenance, content-source administration, quality monitoring, and user support. Business units will also need named content owners to review the accuracy and currency of their approved information.

The technology requirement is an enterprise AI platform or approved cloud service that supports identity integration, access-aware retrieval, encryption, audit logging, usage monitoring, and administrative controls. The project should budget separately for platform licensing or consumption, integration work, security testing, and employee support. Final costs should be confirmed during discovery against the organization’s chosen platform, usage assumptions, retention requirements, and existing infrastructure.

## Governance and risk management

A cross-functional governance group will oversee scope, approved use cases, content-source onboarding, and material changes to the service. Security and privacy reviews will confirm that the assistant honors existing permissions, limits retention to approved purposes, and does not use organizational data to train a general-purpose model unless separately authorized. Logs and monitoring will be designed to support service quality and incident response while following organizational privacy and retention policies.

The assistant will make clear that its responses may be incomplete or incorrect, cite the internal sources used where possible, and direct employees to authoritative channels when the available evidence is insufficient or the question is consequential. Employees will receive practical guidance on appropriate use, verification, and reporting problems. A defined incident process will enable the organization to pause a source or capability if a security, privacy, or material quality issue is identified.

## Success criteria

Within 90 days of broad launch, the project will target at least 60% monthly active use among eligible employees and an average satisfaction rating of at least 4.0 out of 5 among users who provide feedback. Evaluation of representative, high-priority questions should show that at least 80% of answers meet the organization’s quality threshold, with source citations present for at least 90% of answers that rely on internal knowledge.

For selected workflows, controlled measurement should demonstrate a median reduction of at least 20% in time spent finding information or completing the targeted task, compared with a pre-launch baseline. The service must also pass access-control and security testing before each rollout gate, maintain a documented process for correcting or removing unreliable content, and have no unresolved critical data-exposure incidents at the end of the initial operating period.

These measures will be reviewed alongside qualitative feedback and operational data. If adoption, answer quality, or safety falls short, the team will address the cause and repeat the relevant evaluation before expanding the assistant’s capabilities or adding new data sources.

# Proposal: Deployment of an Internal AI Assistant

## Background

Employees across a 5,000-person organization spend significant time searching for policies, procedures, technical guidance, and other internal information. The answers are often spread across multiple systems, and employees may need to interrupt colleagues or submit support requests to find them. A secure internal AI assistant can make approved organizational knowledge easier to access and help employees with routine tasks such as summarizing documents and drafting communications.

This proposal recommends a phased deployment of an internal assistant grounded in the organization’s approved information sources. The assistant will provide responses with links or citations to supporting material, respect existing access permissions, and make clear when it cannot provide a reliable answer. The deployment will begin with low-risk, high-value use cases and expand only after security, quality, and adoption have been demonstrated.

## Objectives

The project will give employees a consistent, convenient way to find and use organizational knowledge; reduce time spent on routine information searches and common support requests; and establish a governed, secure foundation for responsible use of AI. It will also build employee confidence through transparent answers, clear guidance on appropriate use, and a straightforward way to report incorrect or unhelpful responses.

The initial service will support questions about approved policies, procedures, benefits, IT support, and other selected internal knowledge. It will also assist with general-purpose tasks such as summarizing supplied text and drafting or rewriting content. In its initial release, the assistant will not make decisions on behalf of the organization, provide authoritative legal or medical advice, or take actions in business systems without human review.

## Scope

The project includes selecting and configuring the AI platform, integrating it with the organization’s identity and access-management controls, and connecting a prioritized set of approved knowledge sources. Content will be indexed in a way that preserves source permissions, and responses will include citations or links where available. The service will be accessible through an approved employee interface, such as the organization’s intranet or collaboration platform.

The scope also includes security and privacy assessment, content preparation, evaluation of response quality, employee communications and training, operational monitoring, and a defined process for reporting and correcting problems. Business owners will review the content sources in their areas and identify material that is outdated, restricted, or unsuitable for use.

The initial release will not include unrestricted access to all company data, automated changes to employee records or financial systems, or high-impact decisions about hiring, performance, compensation, or access to services. Any expansion into these areas will require a separate risk assessment, approval, and human oversight.

## Timeline

The deployment is expected to take approximately 24 weeks from project approval to organization-wide availability. During weeks one through four, the project team will confirm use cases, establish governance, select the platform and hosting approach, complete initial privacy and security reviews, and agree on success measures. In weeks five through ten, the team will prepare the first knowledge sources, configure identity and permission controls, build the employee interface, and establish logging, monitoring, and feedback processes.

Weeks eleven through fourteen will be used for technical testing, security validation, and evaluation against a representative set of employee questions. A pilot of approximately 300 to 500 employees will then run for six weeks. The pilot will include a cross-section of roles and departments, with regular review of usage, answer quality, safety issues, and user feedback. The project team will address material issues before a broader release.

During weeks twenty-one through twenty-four, the service will be opened to the full organization in controlled stages, supported by training, communications, and help-desk guidance. The first 90 days after launch will serve as a stabilization period, with regular reporting and prioritized improvements to content, prompts, integrations, and user support.

## Resource Requirements

The project will require a core team of approximately 9 to 12 full-time-equivalent staff during implementation. This team should include a project or product lead, AI or platform engineers, integration and identity specialists, data or knowledge engineers, a security and privacy lead, a quality and evaluation lead, and change-management and communications support. Some roles may be provided by existing technology teams or contracted specialists, depending on internal capacity.

Business-area content owners and subject-matter experts will be needed part time to select, review, and maintain knowledge sources and to validate answers in their domains. Legal, privacy, information security, records management, accessibility, procurement, and employee-support teams should participate in reviews at defined project gates. After launch, the organization should retain a smaller ongoing service team responsible for platform operations, content quality, model and prompt changes, incident response, and user feedback.

The organization will also need an approved AI platform and the associated hosting, licensing, or usage capacity; secure connections to selected knowledge repositories; identity-management integration; monitoring and evaluation tooling; and time for employee training. Platform costs will depend on the chosen provider, usage levels, data-retention terms, and existing enterprise agreements, so they should be confirmed during the first phase before procurement is finalized.

## Governance and Risk Management

A cross-functional governance group should oversee the assistant’s permitted uses, approved data sources, evaluation standards, and change approvals. The service will use the organization’s authentication and authorization controls, and it will not expose content to a user who could not access the original source. Data handling, retention, and use of prompts or responses for model improvement must be documented and reviewed before launch.

The assistant will be evaluated for accuracy, source attribution, inappropriate disclosure, bias, and resistance to malicious or misleading inputs. Employees will be advised not to enter highly sensitive personal, customer, or confidential information unless the system is explicitly approved for that information. The interface will explain that AI-generated responses can be wrong and should be verified for consequential work. A documented process will allow employees to report errors, and the service team will be able to investigate and correct issues.

## Success Criteria

The project will be considered successful if the assistant is available to all intended employees within the approved timeline, passes security and privacy review, and demonstrates reliable access controls. Before wider release, it should achieve at least 85 percent satisfactory responses on a representative evaluation set of approved questions, with citations or source links for answers grounded in internal content. Testing should find no unresolved critical security or privacy issues.

Within six months of organization-wide launch, the target is for at least 60 percent of employees to have tried the assistant and for at least 40 percent to use it monthly. For the supported use cases, the organization should measure a reduction in time spent finding routine information and a reduction in repeat questions or tickets to selected support teams, using pre-launch baselines for comparison. Employee satisfaction should reach at least 4.0 out of 5 among surveyed users, while reported harmful or unauthorized disclosures remain at zero and all reported material errors receive timely review.

Results will be reviewed monthly during the pilot and stabilization period, then quarterly. The organization should use these findings to decide whether to improve the initial service, connect additional knowledge sources, or consider more advanced capabilities. Expansion will be based on demonstrated value, quality, and risk control—not on adoption alone.

A laptop that cannot leave the building because a lab instrument only talks to it over a cable nobody can identify. A department that needs its old machines for one more quarter because the new application is “almost ready,” a phrase with no known expiration date. Someone discovers that the conference-room system has been running on a desktop that was never in the inventory at all. Each exception is small enough to sound reasonable, and together they become the actual project.

This is where the schedule stops being a calendar and starts being a negotiation. You find out who can tolerate a day without a device, which machines have to move together, and whose idea of “standard” includes a printer driver last updated during the previous administration. The refresh succeeds less by getting every box out on time than by making the surprises visible early enough that nobody has to pretend they were surprises.

A laptop that cannot leave a particular region because of a licensing clause. A department that needs its old image for one more quarter, though nobody can say what breaks if it changes. A box of perfectly good machines sitting in a closet because the person who knows how to reassign them is on leave. Each exception is small enough to seem reasonable on its own, which is how they add up to a second refresh cycle running quietly alongside the first.

By the time the last device is accounted for, the project has become less about replacing hardware than making decisions visible: who gets an exception, who owns the delay, and what “done” means when there are always three machines somewhere that don’t fit the plan. The spreadsheet still matters. It just turns out the hard part is getting everyone to agree on what the rows mean.

A department has twelve machines that are “mission critical,” though nobody can quite say what mission they’re critical to. One has a label on the lid with a phone number for someone who left in 2019. Another is running a piece of software that only works if you don’t update the operating system, and the person who knows why is on vacation until Thursday. By then, the replacement models have arrived, the old ones are still in use, and somebody has opened a ticket asking whether the new laptops can be made to look like the old ones.

This is where the refresh stops being a hardware project and becomes a project about memory. The inventory tells you what you own; it doesn’t tell you what people depend on, what they’ve quietly worked around, or which “temporary” arrangement has been in place long enough to acquire a budget code. You can still finish on schedule, of course. You just have to decide which surprises count as delays, and which ones were apparently part of the plan all along.

A few machines are still running the one application nobody can name but everyone agrees is essential. Someone’s laptop is technically eligible for replacement, except it belongs to a contractor whose manager left in March. The new model ships with a different port configuration, which means the dock order is now wrong, and the dock order was bundled with a contract that procurement says can’t be amended until next quarter.

By the time the rollout reaches the people who planned it, the schedule has become less a plan than a record of what everyone thought would happen. You start tracking the exceptions separately, then the exceptions to the exceptions. The work is still manageable, but it has stopped being about buying computers. It’s about finding out how the organization actually works.

# Project Proposal: Internal AI Assistant for a 5,000-Employee Organization

## Background

Employees spend significant time searching for information across company systems, interpreting internal guidance, drafting routine communications, and resolving common HR and IT questions. An internal AI assistant can make these activities faster and more consistent by giving employees a simple, conversational way to find approved information and complete everyday knowledge-work tasks.

The assistant will be designed for organizational use, with access governed by each employee’s existing permissions. It will draw on approved internal sources, provide links or citations for answers based on company knowledge, and make clear when it cannot answer confidently. It will support employees rather than replace their judgment: people will remain responsible for decisions and for reviewing AI-generated content before acting on it.

## Objectives

The project will deliver a secure, useful assistant that employees can access through an agreed primary workplace channel. It will help employees find and understand internal information, summarize documents, draft and revise routine content, and resolve common questions using approved knowledge sources.

The deployment will also establish the governance and operating capabilities needed to use AI responsibly at scale. These will include permission-aware access, privacy and security controls, content ownership, quality evaluation, employee guidance, and a process for reporting and correcting problems. The organization will use the rollout to measure whether the assistant produces meaningful improvements in employee experience and time spent on selected tasks.

## Scope

The initial release will serve all 5,000 employees, with access enabled in stages. It will connect to a defined set of approved, high-value sources, such as the intranet, policy and procedure libraries, HR and IT knowledge bases, and selected document repositories. Source selection will be based on business value, content quality, data classification, and integration readiness.

Initial capabilities will include conversational search with source references, summarization of approved internal documents, drafting and editing of routine business content, and responses to common HR and IT questions. The assistant will respect the access controls of connected systems and will not expose information to users who lack permission to view it at the source. Content owners will be responsible for maintaining the accuracy and currency of their material.

The first release will not make decisions or take consequential actions on behalf of employees. It will not be used to make hiring, performance, disciplinary, medical, legal, credit, or other high-impact decisions. It will not autonomously approve transactions, change employee records, or send external communications. Any later expansion into workflow actions will require a separate assessment, authorization, and human-approval design.

## Delivery Timeline

The project is expected to take nine months to reach organization-wide deployment, followed by three months of structured optimization.

During months one and two, the project team will confirm business priorities, identify the first knowledge sources, document requirements, and establish security, privacy, legal, and AI-governance controls. The team will define baseline measures for current task time, employee experience, and relevant support demand. It will also select the platform and integration approach, subject to architecture review and procurement.

During months three and four, the team will build the initial service, connect the first approved sources, implement identity and permission controls, and create the evaluation and monitoring framework. A representative test set will be developed to assess response quality, source attribution, safety, and performance before employees are invited to use the system.

During months five and six, a pilot of approximately 300 to 500 employees will test the assistant across a range of functions and job types. Pilot participants will receive brief training and clear guidance on appropriate use. Feedback, usage data, answer evaluations, and support requests will be reviewed regularly. The team will resolve high-priority issues and refine the product before expanding access.

During months seven and eight, access will expand in successive employee cohorts. The rollout will include communications, short learning materials, manager guidance, and a defined channel for feedback and incident reporting. Additional sources will be connected only after they pass readiness and access-control checks.

In month nine, the assistant will be made available to the full organization, supported by service-desk processes, operational monitoring, and named content owners. Months ten through twelve will focus on improving answer quality, addressing adoption barriers, reviewing benefits against the baseline, and deciding which additional sources or capabilities should be considered next.

## Resource Requirements

The implementation is expected to require a core team of approximately 12 to 15 full-time equivalents during delivery. The team will include a product owner and program manager; AI and application engineers; data and search specialists; integration engineers; user-experience and research support; quality and evaluation specialists; and dedicated security, privacy, architecture, and AI-governance input. Some of these responsibilities may be combined or supplied by existing teams.

Business functions will provide part-time subject-matter experts and content owners, particularly for HR, IT, legal, finance, and other knowledge areas included in the initial release. Their responsibilities will include validating priority use cases, reviewing source material, assessing representative answers, and keeping authoritative content current. Managers and employee representatives will also contribute to pilot feedback and change planning.

After launch, the organization should plan for a standing service team of approximately four to six full-time equivalents, adjusted based on usage and service levels. This team will manage product improvements, integrations, evaluation, incident response, user support, and coordination with content owners. Additional platform, model, storage, and licensing costs will depend on the selected technology, consumption, and existing enterprise agreements; these costs should be confirmed during the first phase and reviewed against measured benefits before expansion.

## Governance and Risk Management

The assistant will use the organization’s approved identity and access-management controls, and connected sources will be reviewed before indexing or use. The project will apply data minimization, retention, logging, and vendor-review requirements consistent with organizational policy. Sensitive or restricted information will be excluded unless the organization has explicitly approved the use case and appropriate safeguards.

Responses will be evaluated for accuracy, relevance, appropriate refusal, and correct source attribution. Employees will be told that AI responses may be incomplete or incorrect and that important decisions require verification against authoritative sources. A named process will allow users to report inaccurate or unsafe answers, and serious privacy, security, or policy incidents will trigger established escalation procedures. Governance owners will review performance and incidents regularly and may pause a capability or source if risks are not adequately controlled.

## Success Criteria

By the end of the first year, the deployment will target at least 70 percent monthly active use among employees who have access, with at least 80 percent of surveyed users rating the assistant as useful for their work. In the pilot and subsequent evaluation, selected tasks such as finding a policy, resolving a common service question, or preparing a routine document should show a measurable reduction in completion time, with a target of at least 20 percent for the workflows where a reliable baseline can be established.

The assistant should achieve at least 90 percent acceptable performance on a curated evaluation set for approved knowledge questions, and at least 95 percent of knowledge-based responses should provide a usable source reference where a source is available. The service should maintain 99.5 percent availability during agreed operating hours. There must be no critical incidents involving unauthorized disclosure of information, and all material quality, privacy, security, and employee-feedback issues must be tracked through to resolution.

Success will be assessed through usage analytics, controlled task studies, employee surveys, support data, evaluation results, and incident records. The executive sponsor and governance group will review these measures at the end of the pilot, at organization-wide launch, and after the first year to determine whether to sustain, adjust, or expand the service.

# Project Proposal: Internal AI Assistant for a 5,000-Employee Organization

## Background

Employees spend significant time searching across internal systems, locating current policies, and repeating routine drafting and summarization work. Knowledge is distributed across multiple repositories, and employees may not always know which source is authoritative. An internal AI assistant can make approved organizational knowledge easier to access and help employees complete common knowledge-work tasks more efficiently.

This proposal recommends deploying a secure, organization-wide assistant that works within existing identity and data-access controls. It will support employees by finding and summarizing internal information, drafting content, and answering questions with links to source material. It will augment employees’ work, not replace their judgment or make consequential decisions on their behalf.

## Objectives

The project will provide employees with a reliable, easy-to-use way to search approved internal knowledge and receive useful answers grounded in organizational sources. It will reduce time spent on selected routine tasks, improve the consistency of answers to common questions, and help employees discover relevant policies, procedures, and guidance.

The deployment will also establish durable governance for enterprise AI use. This includes clear rules for data handling, human review, monitoring, and escalation; controls to ensure employees see only information they are authorized to access; and a feedback process that supports continuous improvement.

## Scope

The project will configure and deploy an enterprise AI assistant for all 5,000 employees. Initial capabilities will include natural-language search and question answering over approved internal content, source-linked summaries, and assistance with drafting and rewriting routine workplace materials. Initial knowledge sources may include approved policy, intranet, IT support, and HR guidance repositories, subject to data-owner approval and technical readiness.

The assistant will use organizational sign-in and permission controls, and its responses to knowledge questions will link to their sources so employees can verify the information. The project will establish content ownership, access rules, retention and logging practices, user guidance, and a process for reporting inaccurate or inappropriate responses. Integration with additional repositories will proceed only after their permissions and data quality have been validated.

The initial release will not authorize the assistant to make employment, financial, legal, medical, or other high-impact decisions. It will not autonomously send external communications, change business records, or execute consequential transactions. Employees will remain responsible for reviewing AI-generated content before relying on or sharing it. Sensitive or restricted information will be available only where the relevant access controls have been tested and approved.

## Timeline

The project is expected to take 24 weeks from approval, followed by a 90-day stabilization period. During weeks 1–4, the project team will confirm priority use cases, identify participating business owners, assess knowledge sources, establish baselines, and approve security, privacy, and governance requirements.

During weeks 5–10, the team will configure the assistant, establish identity and access controls, connect the first approved repositories, and develop employee guidance and support processes. Weeks 11–14 will be used for a controlled pilot with approximately 300 employees across representative functions. The pilot will test answer quality, access controls, usability, and support readiness.

During weeks 15–18, the team will address pilot findings and expand access in stages to approximately 1,000–2,000 employees. The remaining employees will be onboarded during weeks 19–24, with communications, training, and support scaled alongside adoption. The subsequent 90-day stabilization period will focus on resolving issues, improving content coverage, measuring outcomes, and prioritizing enhancements.

## Resource Requirements

The project will require an executive sponsor, a product owner, and a cross-functional delivery team with approximately 8–10 full-time-equivalent staff during implementation. The core team should include a technical lead, two platform or integration engineers, one or two knowledge and data specialists, a change and training lead, and a support or service-management lead. Security, privacy, legal, procurement, accessibility, and records-management specialists should participate on a part-time basis at key design and approval points.

Business units will need to provide accountable owners for connected content, subject-matter experts to validate common questions, and employee champions to support local adoption. The organization will also need capacity for service-desk coverage, platform administration, ongoing content maintenance, and model and security monitoring after launch.

The budget should cover enterprise platform licensing for up to 5,000 employees, implementation and integration work, security and privacy review, training and communications, and ongoing operational support. Licensing and infrastructure costs should be confirmed during procurement, based on the selected platform, usage assumptions, integrations, and retention requirements.

## Success Criteria

Success will be assessed against baselines gathered during discovery and the pilot. Within 90 days of organization-wide rollout, the project will target at least 60% monthly active use, with adoption reported by business unit and role to identify groups needing additional support. In representative tasks such as finding a policy, preparing a routine summary, or drafting a standard response, users should complete work at least 20% faster than the measured baseline without a reduction in quality.

At least 80% of sampled answers to internal knowledge questions should be rated correct and useful by reviewers or users, and at least 95% of those answers should include a usable source link. All tested access-control scenarios must pass before general availability, with no material unauthorized disclosure of internal information. The organization will also target an average user satisfaction rating of at least 4 out of 5, timely resolution of reported issues, and no unresolved high-severity safety, privacy, or security findings at launch.

These measures will be reviewed regularly by the project’s governance group. The group will use employee feedback, performance data, and incident reports to decide whether to expand content sources, revise guidance, or adjust the assistant’s capabilities.

The project’s final evaluation will compare outcomes against the baselines established during discovery. Expansion into additional data sources or action-taking workflows will be recommended only where the evidence shows clear employee value and the relevant security, privacy, and governance controls are in place.

# Proposal: Deploying an Internal AI Assistant

## Background

Employees across a 5,000-person organization spend significant time searching for information, summarizing documents, drafting routine communications, and navigating internal processes. Relevant knowledge is often spread across collaboration platforms, shared drives, intranet pages, and business systems. At the same time, employees may turn to unapproved AI tools when sanctioned options are unavailable, creating avoidable risks to confidential information and regulatory compliance.

A centrally managed internal AI assistant can make approved organizational knowledge easier to use and help employees complete common tasks more efficiently.
