## Objectives

The project will deliver a secure, accessible AI assistant for employees, with a consistent experience across supported devices. The assistant will help employees find and understand approved internal information, summarize and draft content, and complete selected routine tasks. Responses that draw on internal sources will include citations or links where technically feasible, so employees can verify the underlying information.

The deployment will protect organizational data through identity-based access, permission-aware search, appropriate retention and logging controls, and clear restrictions on how employee prompts and organizational content may be used. It will also establish governance, support, and measurement processes that enable the service to improve over time without compromising privacy or security.

## Scope

The first release will provide conversational assistance, search across a defined set of approved internal knowledge sources, and support for common writing and summarization tasks. Initial integrations will include the organization’s identity and access-management service, collaboration and document platforms, intranet, and selected knowledge or service-management systems. The assistant will respect each user’s existing access permissions and direct employees to source material when an answer relies on internal content.

The project includes platform selection or configuration, integration and security engineering, content-readiness work, user research, testing, employee communications, training, and operational support. It also includes a governance model covering acceptable use, data handling, quality review, incident response, and the process for approving new data sources and capabilities.

The initial deployment will not authorize the assistant to make consequential employment, financial, legal, medical, or other high-impact decisions. It will not autonomously execute sensitive transactions or replace required professional review. Any later expansion into workflow automation will require a separate risk assessment, approval, and release plan.

## Delivery Approach and Timeline

The project is expected to take approximately eight months from approval to organization-wide availability. During the first month, the project team will confirm business priorities, establish governance, assess candidate platforms and data sources, define the security and privacy requirements, and record baseline measures for current employee workflows.

In months two and three, the team will configure the service and establish identity, access, logging, and data-retention controls. It will connect the first approved knowledge sources, test permission enforcement, prepare employee guidance, and create a representative evaluation set for answer quality, citation accuracy, and safety. A readiness review at the end of this phase will determine whether the service is suitable for a controlled pilot.

During month four, a pilot of approximately 300 to 500 employees will test the assistant across a range of roles and business areas. The pilot will measure usefulness, answer quality, reliability, and user confidence, while capturing issues through a dedicated feedback and support process. The team will resolve material security, usability, and content problems before expanding access.

In months five and six, access will expand in stages to approximately 1,500 to 2,500 employees. Each stage will follow a readiness check covering system performance, support capacity, user feedback, and the quality of connected content. Months seven and eight will complete the rollout to all 5,000 employees, supported by role-appropriate training, communications, service-desk readiness, and ongoing measurement. Expansion may be paused if a release gate is not met.

## Resource Requirements

The project will require a cross-functional core team, averaging approximately 10 to 14 full-time-equivalent roles during delivery, with peak effort during integration, pilot, and rollout. The team will include a product owner and program manager; solution and security architects; AI, integration, and platform engineers; data and knowledge-management specialists; user-experience and accessibility support; privacy, legal, and risk representatives; change-management and training leads; analytics support; and service-desk representatives.

Business units will provide subject-matter experts to identify priority use cases, validate content, and participate in testing. Executive sponsorship will be needed to set priorities, resolve cross-functional issues, and reinforce responsible use. The organization will also need a platform and hosting budget sized to the selected service, the expected usage pattern, integration and monitoring costs, and ongoing support. Final cost estimates should be established during discovery after platform and licensing options have been assessed.

## Success Criteria

The deployment will be considered successful when the assistant is available to all 5,000 employees, operates within approved security and privacy controls, and has an established owner and support model. Before broad release, testing must confirm that users cannot retrieve information they are not authorized to access, that priority data sources are covered by documented ownership and quality processes, and that critical security or privacy issues have been resolved.

Within 90 days of organization-wide rollout, the project will target at least 60% monthly active use among employees with access, with adoption reviewed by role and business area to identify gaps. In sampled priority tasks, employees should report a 20% or greater reduction in time spent finding information or producing routine first drafts compared with the baseline. At least 75% of surveyed active users should rate the assistant as useful for their work, and at least 80% of evaluated answers grounded in internal sources should be judged accurate and supported by appropriate citations or links.

Operational measures will include service availability, response time, support-ticket volume, resolution time, user feedback, and the rate of harmful or materially incorrect responses. Targets will be finalized during discovery and monitored after launch. The project will also track compliance with approved use and data-handling requirements, with a defined process for investigating incidents and correcting or withdrawing unreliable content or capabilities.

A machine that was supposed to be a standard laptop turns out to run the one application nobody has touched in seven years, but which apparently cannot be touched now. Someone is working from a site with unreliable shipping. Someone else has a dock that only works with the old model, and the dock is technically owned by a different department. None of these are large problems on their own. Together, they become a second project, running alongside the one in the spreadsheet.

The useful thing to refresh, it turns out, is not just the fleet but your understanding of it. Keep a little room in the schedule for the machines that come back late, the records that don’t match, and the perfectly reasonable person who asks whether they can have one more month. The plan still matters. It just works better when it leaves space for the parts nobody could have planned.

The first one is a machine that runs a piece of software nobody can name, but everyone agrees is essential. The second belongs to someone who is on leave until the end of the quarter. Then you discover that the new model has one fewer port, which means a modest refresh has quietly become a docking-station refresh, a cable refresh, and a meeting about whether the existing monitors are now “end of life.”

By the time the last device is swapped, the spreadsheet has acquired several tabs and a color scheme that suggests confidence rather than certainty. None of this means the plan failed. It means the plan met the organization. The useful question is not how to prevent exceptions, but whether you left enough time, budget, and spare chargers for them.

A department has a “temporary” app that only runs on the old image. Someone’s laptop is technically due for replacement but currently lives in a locked cabinet three time zones away. The new model has the right specs, except the dock does not, and the dock is attached to a monitor arm that Facilities installed in 2019 and has no intention of revisiting. None of these are large problems on their own. Together, they turn a clean rollout into a small archaeology project.

So the real work is less about buying machines than finding out how people actually use them, which is rarely the same as what the asset system says. Build time for that discovery, make room for the odd cases, and resist the urge to declare victory when the boxes arrive. A refresh is finished when the old devices are accounted for, the new ones are working, and nobody is quietly keeping a laptop under their desk “just in case.”

A department has a critical app that only runs on the old image. Someone’s laptop is in a repair depot; someone else is on parental leave until the rollout window closes. The new model is technically compatible with the dock, except for the docks installed in three conference rooms, which were bought during a different refresh cycle and have since acquired the status of permanent infrastructure.

So the real work becomes keeping two inventories honest: the one in the spreadsheet and the one that exists in people’s heads. You negotiate extensions, chase approvals, label boxes, and learn which exceptions are harmless and which are holding up an entire team. By the time the last machine is swapped, the next refresh is already on the calendar—and the spreadsheet looks decisive again.

# Project Proposal: Deployment of an Internal AI Assistant

## Background

This proposal recommends deploying a centrally managed AI assistant for the organization’s 5,000 employees over a 26-week implementation. Employees routinely spend time searching across internal resources, resolving recurring questions, and drafting or summarizing routine communications. At the same time, the convenience of public AI tools can encourage unapproved use and create risks to confidential information. A secure internal assistant would offer a governed alternative while making approved organizational knowledge easier to use.

The assistant will provide responses based on approved internal sources where available, link users to those sources, and support routine drafting and summarization. It will be designed as an aid to employees—not as a source of record or a substitute for professional judgment.

## Objectives

The project will make approved internal knowledge faster to find, reduce time spent on common information and writing tasks, and provide employees with a consistent, secure way to use generative AI at work. It will also establish a sustainable operating model for evaluating AI quality, managing risks, and improving the service over time.

Success depends not only on deploying the technology but also on employees understanding its capabilities and limitations. The project will therefore pair the assistant with practical training, clear usage guidance, and an easy way to report incorrect or unhelpful responses.

## Scope and safeguards

The first release will be available to employees through a centrally managed interface using corporate sign-in. It will answer questions about approved policies, procedures, and frequently asked questions; search and summarize approved internal documents; and help draft or revise routine internal content. It will connect initially to a limited set of well-governed knowledge sources, such as selected HR and IT guidance and corporate policy repositories. The final sources and any collaboration-platform integration will be confirmed during discovery.

Access to connected content will follow employees’ existing permissions. The service will use an enterprise-managed AI platform under terms that prevent company prompts and retrieved content from being used to train shared public models. Logging, retention, and monitoring will be minimized and defined with security, privacy, legal, and records-management teams. Usage analytics will be aggregated for service improvement and will not be used to assess individual employee performance.

The first release will not make or recommend employment, legal, financial, medical, or other high-impact decisions. It will not autonomously send communications, change business systems, or take actions on an employee’s behalf. Highly restricted or regulated information will remain out of scope unless separately reviewed and approved. Employees will be told that AI-generated content can be wrong, and they will be expected to verify outputs before relying on them—particularly for external communications or material business decisions. When the assistant lacks adequate source support, it should say so and direct the employee to a relevant source or human support channel.

A cross-functional steering group, including IT, security, privacy, legal, HR, records management, and business representatives, will approve connected sources, review evaluation results, oversee incident handling, and decide whether the service is ready to advance at each project gate.

## Timeline

The project will run for 26 weeks. During weeks 1–4, the team will confirm priority use cases, establish baseline measures, select or validate the enterprise platform, assess candidate knowledge sources, and agree on security, privacy, retention, and acceptable-use requirements. This phase will also confirm licensing and operating costs.

During weeks 5–10, the team will configure the assistant, implement corporate sign-in and permission-aware retrieval, connect the initial approved sources, and prepare a representative set of test questions. Security and privacy reviews, access-control testing, and evaluation of response quality will be completed before employee testing begins.

During weeks 11–16, a pilot of approximately 300–500 employees will test the service across several functions and job levels. The team will review user feedback, answer quality, citations, support demand, and potential risks, then make changes before broader release. Expansion will proceed only if the agreed quality, security, and usability gates are met.

During weeks 17–22, the assistant will be rolled out in waves to the remaining employee population, supported by targeted training, manager communications, and a network of employee champions. Weeks 23–26 will focus on stabilizing operations, resolving recurring issues, reviewing the initial performance scorecard, and agreeing on the next set of improvements.

This schedule assumes that the platform decision can be made within the first four weeks and that the selected knowledge sources have usable permissions and ownership. Any significant delay or source-quality issue should be addressed at a steering-group gate rather than by bypassing review.

## Resource requirements

The project will require an average of approximately 8–9 full-time-equivalent staff during delivery. This capacity should include a product and program lead; two AI application and engineering specialists; one to one-and-a-half platform and integration specialists; fractional security and privacy, legal, procurement, and records-management support; a knowledge and content lead; a change-management and training lead; analytics and service-support capacity; and pooled subject-matter expertise from HR, IT, operations, and business teams. An executive sponsor and cross-functional steering group will provide oversight at key decisions.

A network of approximately 25–40 employee champions will help test the assistant, gather feedback, and support adoption within their teams. After launch, the organization should retain approximately 2–3 full-time-equivalent staff across product ownership, platform operations, knowledge management, security review, analytics, and user support. The exact ongoing level will depend on adoption and service demand.

The budget should cover enterprise licensing sized for up to 5,000 employees, AI usage, integrations, security and quality testing, employee training, and ongoing support. Procurement should confirm vendor-specific costs during the first phase; no platform or pricing assumption is made in this proposal.

## Success criteria

The project will establish baselines during discovery and track results through pilot and rollout. Proposed targets, to be confirmed in the first four weeks, are that the assistant achieves at least 90% accuracy on a representative, human-reviewed set of in-scope questions and that at least 95% of evaluated knowledge-grounded responses provide valid citations. Any critical unsafe response or confirmed unauthorized access will block expansion until resolved.

Within 90 days of organization-wide rollout, the target is for at least 60% of employees to use the assistant monthly and 35% to use it weekly. At least 80% of surveyed users should rate the service useful, with an average usefulness rating of at least 4 out of 5. The assistant should reduce median completion time by at least 20% on a defined set of common knowledge-finding tasks compared with the prelaunch baseline. For HR and IT inquiry categories directly addressed by the assistant, the organization should also aim for a 10% reduction in avoidable repeat inquiries, adjusted for seasonal changes and employee volume.

Operational targets are at least 99.5% monthly availability and zero material privacy or security incidents attributable to the service. Results will be reviewed through a privacy-conscious dashboard combining technical measures, independent quality checks, user feedback, and business-task outcomes.

Approval of this proposal authorizes a six-month, gated implementation within the scope described above. At the end of week 26, the steering group will assess the results and recommend whether to continue, expand the connected knowledge sources, or revise the service before further investment.

# Project Proposal: Internal AI Assistant for a 5,000-Employee Organization

## Background and Rationale

Employees across a 5,000-person organization routinely search policies, procedures, technical guidance, and internal knowledge spread across multiple systems. They also spend time drafting routine communications and summarizing documents. These tasks create avoidable delays, repeat questions to support teams, and make it harder to find consistent, up-to-date information.

An internal AI assistant can make approved organizational knowledge easier to use and help employees with common writing and information tasks. Unlike a general-purpose public chatbot, the proposed assistant will operate within the organization’s security and identity controls, retrieve only content each employee is authorized to access, and cite its sources. It will support employees rather than replace their judgment or make decisions on the organization’s behalf.

## Objectives

The project will deliver a secure, accessible assistant that helps employees find and understand approved internal information, draft and summarize routine content, and complete selected knowledge-based tasks more efficiently. It will establish clear ownership for the assistant’s content, model, security controls, and ongoing evaluation. It will also provide reliable evidence of employee adoption, answer quality, productivity impact, and operating cost so leaders can decide how to improve or expand the service.

## Scope and Operating Model

The initial release will be available to all employees through a secure interface selected during platform evaluation, using the organization’s existing single sign-on and identity controls. It will support questions and answers grounded in approved internal sources, with links or citations to the material used. Initial sources should include selected intranet content, policies, procedures, IT and employee-service guidance, and approved templates. Users may also use it to draft, rewrite, and summarize routine work content, with responsibility for reviewing outputs remaining with the user.

Every connected source must retain its existing access permissions; the assistant must not expose information a user could not otherwise access. The selected platform must meet organizational requirements for encryption, data residency, retention, auditability, and privacy. Prompts and organizational content must not be used to train a public or shared model. Logging and analytics will be limited to what is needed for security, service improvement, and approved measurement, with retention governed by organizational policy.

The first release will not make employment, financial, legal, medical, or other high-impact decisions, nor will it take autonomous actions or write to business systems. General policy information may be in scope where it is supported by approved sources, but individual cases requiring professional judgment must be referred to the appropriate team. New integrations or actions will require a separate risk review and approval. Employees will receive clear guidance on appropriate use, known limitations, and how to report incorrect or unsafe responses.

A cross-functional governance group led by an executive sponsor will oversee launch decisions, risk, and outcomes. It will include representatives from IT, security, privacy, legal, HR or other relevant business functions, and communications. Named content owners will be responsible for the accuracy and freshness of each connected source.

## Timeline

The proposed implementation will take approximately eight months. During the first month, the organization will confirm priority use cases, establish governance and baseline measurements, assess candidate platforms, and select the initial content sources. Platform selection will consider security and privacy controls, integration effort, usability, model performance, scalability, support, and total cost.

During months two and three, the project team will configure the service, implement identity and permission-aware retrieval, connect the initial content sources, and develop a representative test set of common employee questions and tasks. The team will also complete privacy, security, accessibility, and operational reviews before any employee pilot.

During months four and five, a pilot of approximately 300–500 employees will test the assistant across a range of roles and work patterns. The pilot will include onboarding, feedback channels, quality reviews, security testing, and measurement against the agreed baseline. Expansion will proceed only after the organization confirms that the assistant meets its quality and safety gates and that key issues have been resolved.

During months six through eight, access will expand in waves until the service is available to all 5,000 employees. Each wave will be supported by targeted communications, training, help-desk readiness, and monitoring of service quality and usage. After broad release, the team will continue to review performance, refresh connected content, and assess additional use cases through the governance process.

## Resource Requirements

Plan for a cross-functional implementation team averaging approximately 10–14 full-time-equivalent staff, with additional part-time participation from business content owners. The core team should include a program and product lead, an AI or solution architect, three to five platform and integration engineers, data or content specialists, security and privacy expertise, user-experience and evaluation support, and change-management, training, and service-support capacity. Business teams will need to assign subject-matter experts to validate content, test answers, and resolve ownership or quality issues.

The project budget should cover platform and per-user licensing, model or inference usage, integration and content remediation, security and privacy testing, training and communications, and ongoing service operations. Final costs should be established through platform procurement and refined using pilot usage and support data; the organization should evaluate both launch costs and the recurring cost per active user.

## Success Criteria

Before the pilot expands, a representative benchmark of common, in-scope questions must show that at least 90% of sampled knowledge answers are judged accurate and supported by current approved sources. All connected repositories must pass permission tests, and no critical or high-severity security findings may remain open at a scale-up gate. The pilot must also demonstrate a workable process for reporting, investigating, and correcting problematic responses.

Six months after organization-wide release, the target is for at least 60% of employees to be monthly active users, with at least 80% of surveyed users rating the assistant useful for their work. For three or more agreed, high-volume tasks, the organization should demonstrate at least a 15% reduction in median completion time without a decline in output quality. Participating service teams should also track changes in repetitive, in-scope enquiries against their baseline. The service should maintain at least 99.5% monthly availability and have no unresolved severe privacy or security incidents attributable to the assistant.

Measures will be reviewed through aggregate service analytics, task-based evaluation, user feedback, and operational reporting, with appropriate privacy safeguards. These targets will guide investment decisions and ongoing improvement rather than serve as claims of guaranteed benefit.

Approval is requested for an eight-month, stage-gated implementation, an executive sponsor, the cross-functional team described above, and a 300–500-person pilot. This approach provides a controlled path to organization-wide access while making security, answer quality, employee value, and operating cost explicit conditions of success.

# Project Proposal: Internal AI Assistant for a 5,000-Employee Organization

Approval is requested for a 24-week initiative to design, pilot, and deploy a secure internal AI assistant for all 5,000 employees. The assistant will make trusted organizational knowledge easier to find and help employees complete routine writing, summarization, and research tasks. It will operate within existing identity and access controls, cite its sources, and keep people responsible for decisions and actions.

## Background

Employees spend time searching across intranets, shared drives, policies, and service portals, or asking colleagues to locate information they cannot readily find. At the same time, employees may turn to public AI tools for help with routine work, creating risks around confidential information, inconsistent answers, and unapproved data use. A centrally managed internal assistant can address both needs: improving access to organizational knowledge while providing clear security, privacy, and usage safeguards.

The assistant will complement existing systems and expertise, not replace them. Its initial purpose is to help employees find and work with approved information more efficiently, with the organization able to measure quality, adoption, and business value before expanding its capabilities.

## Objectives

The project will give employees a straightforward, accessible way to ask questions about approved internal information and receive useful answers with links to supporting sources. It will also help employees summarize authorized documents, draft routine communications, and prepare outlines or meeting materials. The deployment will establish responsible-use guidance, oversight, and support processes from the outset, while providing evidence of whether the assistant reduces effort on selected everyday tasks.

Success will depend not only on usage, but on employees being able to trust the answers, understand their limitations, and use the tool without exposing information to people who are not authorized to see it.

## Scope and safeguards

The first release will provide an internal, single-sign-on assistant through an accessible web interface and, where practical, existing collaboration tools. It will use an approved enterprise AI service with retrieval from selected, organization-approved sources. Initial sources may include current policies, standard operating procedures, HR and IT knowledge articles, and other curated internal reference material. Each source will have an accountable content owner and a process for keeping it current.

The assistant will respect the permissions of the underlying systems: employees will only receive information they are authorized to access. Responses about internal content will cite the relevant source and link to it. When the assistant cannot find a reliable answer, it should say so rather than present speculation as fact. Employees will have a way to provide feedback and report answers that appear incorrect, incomplete, or unsafe.

The initial deployment will not give the assistant authority to execute transactions, send external communications, or make employment, legal, medical, financial, or other high-impact decisions. Sensitive case records and other restricted material will remain out of scope unless separately assessed and approved. Employees will be instructed to review AI-generated material before using it in consequential work.

Security and privacy controls will include identity-based access, encryption, audit and usage logging, retention rules, data-loss protections, and a documented privacy and security assessment. Procurement will confirm that prompts and organizational content are not used to train shared models, and will review provider retention, processing location, and incident-response terms. Testing will cover answer quality, access boundaries, and attempts to elicit restricted or misleading information.

## Timeline

The project will run for 24 weeks, followed by 90 days of post-launch measurement. During weeks one through four, the team will confirm priority use cases, document current task-completion baselines, assess candidate data sources, select the technical approach, and complete initial privacy, security, and procurement reviews. This phase will also establish ownership for the content included in the pilot.

During weeks five through ten, the team will configure the assistant, connect the first approved sources, implement single sign-on and permission-aware retrieval, and build a test set for evaluating answers. The team will also prepare employee guidance, support procedures, and monitoring dashboards. A launch-readiness review at the end of this phase will confirm that core controls are in place before real users are invited.

Weeks eleven through fourteen will be a controlled pilot with approximately 300–400 employees drawn from different functions, roles, and locations. Pilot participants will test the agreed use cases and provide structured feedback. During weeks fifteen through eighteen, the team will address defects, improve source quality and response handling, repeat security and quality testing, and decide whether the solution is ready for wider release.

From weeks nineteen through twenty-four, access will expand in managed waves until the assistant is available across the organization. Training, communications, and employee support will accompany each wave. Following full deployment, the team will monitor adoption, answer quality, incidents, operating costs, and task outcomes for 90 days and report results to the executive sponsor and steering group.

## Resource requirements

The initiative will require an average core team of approximately 10–12 full-time equivalents during the 24-week delivery period. This team should include a product or program lead, a solution architect, two AI engineers, two data and integration engineers, a quality and evaluation analyst, a knowledge or content lead, and a change and training lead. Security, privacy, legal, procurement, platform operations, and service-desk specialists should provide a further one to two full-time equivalents in combined capacity, with appropriate executive sponsorship and business-owner time.

Subject-matter experts from functions such as HR, IT, Operations, Finance, Legal, and Communications will be needed part-time to select use cases, validate sources, and review answers. A network of approximately 20–30 departmental or site champions can support pilot feedback, local communications, and employee onboarding, particularly during rollout.

Funding will be needed for enterprise model access or hosting, search and indexing, system integrations, logging and monitoring, security testing, training, and ongoing service support. Actual software and infrastructure costs will depend on vendor selection, usage, and hosting choices, so procurement should establish unit costs during discovery and forecast the production service against expected use by 5,000 employees. Consumption limits and cost monitoring should be in place before broad release.

## Success criteria

The first four weeks will establish baselines for the selected tasks, and results will be reviewed 90 days after organization-wide deployment. The rollout will be considered successful if at least 95% of employees with corporate accounts can access the assistant and at least 50% of those employees are monthly active users by that review. In a measured comparison with baseline performance, employees should complete the three selected tasks at least 20% faster on average.

Quality and safety will be assessed through both controlled testing and user feedback. At least 90% of evaluated answers about internal policies and procedures should cite a correct, authorized source, and at least 85% of pilot users should rate the assistant’s responses as useful. There must be no unresolved critical security or privacy findings at launch and no confirmed cross-permission disclosure. The production service should achieve at least 99.5% monthly availability, with operating costs within the approved budget.

Adoption, task performance, answer quality, reported issues, and costs will be reviewed regularly after launch. The organization should use those results to decide whether to expand the source content or introduce additional capabilities. This phased approach makes the assistant broadly available while ensuring that further investment is guided by evidence of usefulness, safety, and value.

# Project Proposal: Deployment of an Internal AI Assistant

## Background

Employees across a 5,000-person organization must often search multiple systems to find policies, procedures, technical guidance, and business knowledge. They also spend time drafting routine communications, summarizing information, and turning notes into actionable work. An internal AI assistant can reduce this effort and make trusted knowledge easier to access. Without an approved, governed service, employees may turn to public AI tools, creating risks to confidential information and inconsistent use.

This proposal recommends a secure, organization-wide assistant built on an enterprise-approved AI service. It will retrieve information from selected internal sources, respect existing user permissions, and provide citations so employees can verify answers. The assistant will support employees’ work, not replace subject-matter experts or make decisions on the organization’s behalf.

## Objectives and Scope

The project will provide employees with a simple, consistent way to find and understand approved internal information; reduce time spent on common research, drafting, and summarization tasks; and establish a measurable, secure foundation for future AI-enabled services. Success will depend on trustworthy answers, appropriate data controls, employee adoption, and demonstrable improvements to everyday work.

The initial release will support natural-language questions about selected HR, IT, policy, and business-process information; search and summarize documents a user is authorized to access; and draft routine text or summarize material supplied by the user. Answers will cite their sources and indicate when the assistant cannot provide a well-supported response. Users will also be able to submit feedback and report incorrect or risky answers.

The first release will be assistive and read-only. It will not independently send external communications, change records, approve transactions, or make employment, legal, financial, or other high-impact decisions. Highly restricted or sensitive information will be excluded unless specifically reviewed and approved. The service will use single sign-on, enforce source permissions at retrieval, and apply approved controls for encryption, logging, and retention. Contracts and configuration will prohibit external providers from using organizational data to train their general models.

## Delivery Timeline

The proposed delivery window is 24 weeks from kickoff, followed by a 90-day benefits review. During weeks 1–4, the project team will confirm priority use cases, document baseline task times, identify data owners, assess source quality, and establish security, privacy, legal, and governance requirements. Procurement and technical discovery will begin during this phase so that vendor decisions do not become a late-stage dependency.

During weeks 5–8, the team will finalize the solution architecture, select the approved model and hosting approach, complete risk assessments, and define the first set of data connections. Weeks 9–14 will focus on building the assistant, integrating identity and approved knowledge sources, configuring monitoring, and testing answer quality and access controls.

A cross-functional pilot of approximately 300 employees will run during weeks 15–17. The pilot will test representative tasks, accessibility, answer quality, security, and support processes. If the agreed quality and safety gates are met, the service will expand in controlled waves to approximately 1,500 employees during weeks 18–21. Feedback and operating data from each wave will guide improvements before organization-wide availability, targeted for weeks 22–24. The team will provide enhanced support during rollout and assess benefits 90 days after full launch. If a critical security, privacy, or quality issue arises, expansion will pause until it is resolved.

## Resource Requirements and Operating Model

The project will require a cross-functional core team averaging approximately 12–13 full-time equivalents, with peak staffing of 14–16 during implementation and rollout. This team should include a product owner and program manager; an enterprise architect; AI and application engineers; integration and platform engineers; data and knowledge specialists; a quality and evaluation lead; security and privacy specialists; user experience and accessibility support; and change management, training, and service-desk capacity. Business subject-matter experts and content owners from priority functions will contribute part-time, generally 0.2–0.4 FTE per participating function. Existing staff can fill many of these roles, subject to agreed capacity and ownership.

The technical provision should cover an enterprise AI model or service, secure search and retrieval, approved connectors to internal sources, development and production environments, identity integration, monitoring, and cost controls. The budget should account for implementation effort, model or seat licensing, hosting, connector and search services, security reviews, training, and support. Since usage and licensing costs depend on the selected service and employee behavior, the project should set a spending cap before the pilot and use pilot data to confirm the ongoing cost model. After launch, plan for approximately 3–5 FTE of continuing product, engineering, platform, knowledge-management, and support capacity, adjusted to actual usage and service demand.

A governance group with representatives from IT, security, privacy, legal, HR, records management, and participating business areas will review approved use cases, source permissions, incidents, and launch gates. Named content owners will remain accountable for the accuracy and currency of connected materials.

## Success Criteria

Within 90 days of organization-wide launch, the assistant should reach at least 60% monthly active use and 35% weekly active use among eligible employees, with average user satisfaction of at least 4 out of 5. For four to six agreed high-volume tasks, measurement against the pre-launch baseline should show at least a 20% reduction in median completion time.

On a curated evaluation set covering supported use cases, at least 90% of reviewed answers should be rated accurate and useful, and at least 95% of cited sources should substantiate the claims they accompany. Before broader rollout, all permission-control tests must pass, and there must be no unresolved critical security or privacy findings. After stabilization, the service should target 99.5% monthly availability and response times below 10 seconds at the 95th percentile. Usage and operating costs should remain within the approved budget, with monthly reporting to the governance group.

These measures will determine whether the service is delivering practical value, not simply generating logins. Approval of the proposal should include a named executive sponsor, committed cross-functional capacity, authorization to begin procurement and source reviews, and agreement on the pilot and expansion gates.

One machine is attached to a label printer that only works with a driver nobody can find; another belongs to someone who has been on leave since the inventory was last reconciled. A few have software that was installed by a person who left three years ago and apparently took the instructions with them. Each exception is small enough to sound unreasonable on its own, which is how they survive long enough to arrive all at once.

So the schedule doesn’t really slip. It becomes a second schedule, maintained in a tab nobody meant to create, with owners and caveats and a column labeled “after.” The useful question stops being how many devices shipped and becomes how many people can put the new one on their desk without losing a morning to passwords, peripherals, and archaeology.

One person is on leave until the old machine is meant to be returned; another has a specialist app whose installer lives in an email thread from 2019; someone else insists their monitor is “part of the laptop” because it’s been plugged into the same dock since the last refresh. None of this is difficult on its own. The difficulty is discovering it while the rollout is already moving, and deciding which surprises can wait without turning the help desk into a forwarding address.

Eventually, the schedule stops being a list of serial numbers and becomes a map of dependencies: who needs a loaner, who needs data migrated, which sites need hands on keyboards, and where a spare charger is worth more than another status meeting. The successful refresh isn’t the one with the cleanest spreadsheet. It’s the one that leaves people able to do their jobs on Monday, even if the spreadsheet has quietly acquired three new columns and a tab called “actual plan.”

The first exception is usually software nobody has heard of that turns out to be essential to one person in one office. The next is a laptop that belongs to someone on leave, a dock that works only with the old model, or a department that has quietly built its entire process around a folder named “Final_v7.” None of these things are difficult to fix on their own. The difficulty is discovering them before the old machine is wiped and the person who knows how it works is on a flight.

At that point, the refresh stops being a purchasing exercise and becomes a study in institutional memory. You’re not moving devices so much as finding all the small, informal arrangements that made the old ones useful. The teams that get through it cleanly aren’t the ones with the neatest spreadsheet; they’re the ones who leave enough room for someone to say, “Wait, what happens to the label printer?” before the answer becomes a ticket.

A dock that only negotiates with one model of laptop. A finance team that wants the old machines kept “just in case,” which quietly becomes a second fleet with none of the documentation. Someone in a regional office has a critical application installed by a contractor whose phone number is now a dead link. None of this appears in the spreadsheet, because the spreadsheet describes devices, not the people and habits attached to them.

The work, then, is less about swapping boxes than making change boring. You need a clean inventory, a path for the odd software, a plan for data that can’t simply be copied, and enough slack to absorb the department that misses every deadline until the deadline becomes a production incident. Refresh cycles go well when nothing interesting happens—which usually means someone did a lot of uninteresting work beforehand.
