# Proposal: Enterprise Deployment of an Internal AI Assistant

## Background

Our organization’s employees spend significant time searching for information, drafting routine content, summarizing documents, navigating internal processes, and responding to recurring questions. Knowledge is distributed across collaboration platforms, document repositories, policies, ticketing systems, and business applications, making it difficult for employees to find reliable answers quickly. This fragmentation creates duplicated effort, slows decision-making, increases pressure on support functions, and makes organizational knowledge difficult to scale.

Recent advances in enterprise artificial intelligence make it possible to provide employees with a secure, organization-specific assistant that can answer questions, summarize approved internal content, generate drafts, support common workflows, and guide users to authoritative sources. Deployed responsibly, an internal AI assistant can improve productivity while preserving existing security, privacy, compliance, and records-management requirements.

This proposal recommends deploying an internal AI assistant to all 5,000 employees through a phased implementation. The assistant will be designed as a trusted productivity and knowledge tool, with access controlled according to existing employee permissions and with clear safeguards for sensitive information, human oversight, and responsible use.

## Objectives

The primary objective is to provide every employee with secure, reliable access to an AI assistant that improves how they find information, complete routine work, and interact with internal services.

The program will pursue the following objectives:

- Reduce the time employees spend searching for internal information and producing routine written content.
- Provide consistent, source-grounded answers based on approved organizational knowledge.
- Improve access to policies, procedures, institutional knowledge, and support resources.
- Automate or streamline selected low-risk, high-volume workflows such as drafting, summarization, meeting preparation, knowledge retrieval, and service requests.
- Establish enterprise standards for AI security, privacy, governance, accessibility, and responsible use.
- Build employee confidence and capability through training, guidance, and practical use cases.
- Create a scalable foundation for future AI-enabled business processes and department-specific applications.

The assistant will augment employees rather than replace professional judgment or organizational accountability. It will be positioned as a support tool whose outputs require appropriate review, particularly when they affect customers, employees, finances, legal matters, security, or other high-impact decisions.

## Scope

The initial deployment will make the assistant available to all 5,000 employees through the organization’s approved collaboration and productivity environment, subject to standard identity, access, and acceptable-use controls. The service will support natural-language questions and requests, document summarization, content drafting, information retrieval, translation where appropriate, meeting and project assistance, and guided access to internal policies and services.

The assistant will be connected initially to a curated set of high-value, low- to moderate-risk information sources. These may include corporate policies, employee handbooks, process documentation, approved knowledge bases, IT support articles, frequently asked questions, training materials, and selected departmental repositories. Content will be indexed and surfaced according to existing role-based permissions. The assistant will cite or link to source materials wherever feasible so employees can verify answers and locate authoritative information.

The first release will prioritize use cases that offer broad value without requiring autonomous decision-making. Examples include answering HR and IT policy questions, helping employees locate procedures, drafting internal communications, summarizing approved documents, preparing meeting materials, and assisting with service-desk interactions. Department-specific use cases may be added after the core service has demonstrated acceptable performance and governance controls.

The initial scope will exclude fully autonomous actions in high-risk areas, unsupervised decisions regarding employment or customer eligibility, legal or medical advice, financial commitments, changes to production systems, and access to highly restricted information unless separately approved. Any future expansion into these areas will require additional risk assessment, technical controls, testing, and executive authorization.

The program will include employee communications, training, support procedures, model and content governance, security monitoring, usage analytics, and a process for reporting inaccurate, unsafe, or inappropriate outputs. It will also include an ongoing content-management process to improve the quality, freshness, ownership, and discoverability of the information used by the assistant.

## Delivery Approach and Timeline

The deployment will be completed over approximately nine months, followed by ongoing optimization.

During **Month 1**, the organization will establish program governance, confirm executive sponsorship, define success measures, select the technology approach, and complete an initial assessment of security, privacy, compliance, procurement, and data-protection requirements. Business units will nominate representatives to participate in requirements gathering and use-case prioritization.

During **Months 2 and 3**, the program team will design the target architecture and operating model. This phase will include identity and access integration, data-source inventory, content classification, permission mapping, retention requirements, audit logging, risk controls, and support processes. The team will also prepare the initial knowledge base and define standards for prompt design, response citations, escalation, incident management, and acceptable use.

During **Months 4 and 5**, a controlled pilot will be conducted with approximately 250 to 400 employees representing corporate functions, operational teams, managers, technical users, and nontechnical users. The pilot will focus on priority use cases and will measure answer quality, source accuracy, task completion time, user satisfaction, adoption, and security performance. Pilot participants will receive training and will provide structured feedback. Findings will be used to refine the assistant, improve source content, adjust access controls, and identify use cases that require additional safeguards.

During **Months 6 and 7**, the assistant will be expanded to approximately 1,000 to 1,500 employees across a broader set of departments. This phase will validate performance at greater scale, test support demand, assess training effectiveness, and confirm that the service operates reliably across different business contexts. Departmental champions will help identify practical applications and promote responsible adoption.

During **Months 8 and 9**, the assistant will be rolled out to the remaining employees in waves. Communications will explain the service’s capabilities, limitations, privacy protections, and acceptable-use requirements. Training will be available through short courses, live sessions, quick-reference materials, and embedded guidance. The deployment will include enhanced monitoring during each wave and a formal readiness review before full organizational availability.

After the initial rollout, the organization will operate the assistant as an ongoing enterprise service. Quarterly reviews will evaluate adoption, business value, content quality, security events, user feedback, and new use-case requests. The service roadmap will prioritize improvements based on measurable outcomes and risk, rather than usage volume alone.

## Resource Requirements

The program will require a cross-functional team with sufficient authority to make decisions across technology, operations, risk, and business functions. The core implementation team is expected to include a program director, product manager, enterprise architect, AI or machine-learning engineer, data and knowledge-management specialists, integration engineers, information-security representatives, privacy and legal advisers, user-experience and accessibility specialists, change-management leads, training specialists, analytics support, and service-desk personnel.

A reasonable implementation baseline is approximately 12 to 18 full-time equivalent internal and contracted resources during the design, pilot, and rollout period. After deployment, an ongoing operating team of approximately 6 to 10 full-time equivalent resources is expected, depending on the number of integrations, the breadth of supported content, and the degree of workflow automation. This team will manage product improvements, content quality, model and prompt configuration, access controls, monitoring, user support, training, and governance.

The technology environment will require an enterprise-grade AI platform or approved model service, secure application hosting, identity and single-sign-on integration, role- and attribute-based access controls, data connectors, retrieval and indexing services, logging and monitoring, analytics, and integration with existing collaboration, knowledge-management, and service-management platforms. The selected solution must support contractual protections for organizational data, prohibit unauthorized use of company content for model training, provide administrative controls, and meet applicable security, privacy, accessibility, and regulatory requirements.

Funding will be required for software licensing or consumption, implementation services, integration and data preparation, security and privacy assessments, training and communications, support capacity, user research, and ongoing operations. A contingency reserve should be maintained for unexpected integration complexity, additional data remediation, model evaluation, or changes required to meet compliance and security standards.

Equally important are nontechnical resources. Each major business area should designate a content owner and an AI adoption champion. Content owners will be responsible for ensuring that information is accurate, current, appropriately classified, and approved for use. Adoption champions will provide feedback, identify high-value use cases, support training, and help employees use the assistant effectively.

## Governance, Risk, and Responsible Use

The assistant will operate under an enterprise AI governance framework approved before pilot launch. Governance will define permitted and prohibited use cases, data-handling requirements, human-review obligations, accountability for outputs, vendor and model-management standards, and procedures for reporting and resolving incidents.

Access to information will follow existing organizational permissions. The assistant will not be used to bypass repositories, security groups, confidentiality restrictions, or records-management requirements. Sensitive information will be handled according to established classification and privacy policies, and prompts and responses will be subject to appropriate logging, retention, and monitoring rules.

The assistant will be evaluated for factual accuracy, source attribution, harmful or biased outputs, inappropriate disclosure, prompt-injection risks, unauthorized actions, and resilience against misuse. High-impact outputs will require human review, and the interface will clearly communicate that generated responses may be incomplete or incorrect. Users will be instructed not to treat the assistant as a substitute for professional, legal, financial, medical, safety, or managerial judgment.

A formal feedback and escalation mechanism will allow employees to flag inaccurate answers, missing sources, privacy concerns, or unsafe behavior. Reported issues will be triaged according to severity, with critical issues subject to immediate containment and investigation. Model, prompt, connector, and knowledge-base changes will be managed through documented testing and change-control procedures.

## Success Criteria

The deployment will be considered successful when the assistant is broadly adopted, demonstrably useful, secure, and trusted by employees and business leaders. Success will be measured through a combination of quantitative performance indicators and qualitative feedback.

Within six months of organization-wide availability, the program should achieve active usage by at least 60 percent of employees, with continued monthly use by at least 40 percent. At least 70 percent of surveyed users should report that the assistant saves time or improves the quality of their work, and at least 75 percent should be able to complete core tasks using the assistant after training.

For priority knowledge use cases, the program should achieve at least 85 percent accuracy and source-grounding in evaluated responses, with clear citations or links available for the majority of factual answers. The organization should target a 20 percent reduction in time spent locating routine internal information and a 15 percent reduction in selected service-desk or support requests that can be reliably resolved through approved self-service content.

The service should meet agreed availability and response-time targets, maintain zero critical privacy or security incidents attributable to inadequate deployment controls, and demonstrate that access restrictions are consistently enforced. All priority content sources should have assigned owners, defined review cycles, and documented freshness standards.

Business units should identify and validate at least 20 high-value use cases during the first year, with at least five producing measurable improvements in cycle time, service quality, employee experience, or operating cost. Employee feedback, support trends, risk findings, and usage analytics should be reviewed quarterly, with corrective actions documented and tracked.

## Conclusion

Deploying an internal AI assistant across the organization will create a common, secure foundation for improving employee productivity and access to knowledge. A phased approach will allow the organization to demonstrate value early, manage risk carefully, improve content quality, and build employee trust before scaling to all 5,000 employees. With strong governance, permission-aware data integration, clear human oversight, and sustained investment in adoption and content management, the assistant can become a reliable enterprise service and a platform for future AI-enabled transformation.

# Proposal: Enterprise Deployment of an Internal AI Assistant

## Background

Organizations are increasingly using generative artificial intelligence to improve productivity, accelerate decision-making, and make institutional knowledge easier to access. Within a 5,000-employee organization, employees routinely spend significant time searching for information, drafting routine communications, summarizing documents, preparing reports, responding to internal questions, and navigating policies and procedures. These activities represent substantial opportunities for efficiency gains, provided that AI is deployed securely, responsibly, and in a way that complements—rather than replaces—employee expertise.

This proposal recommends the phased deployment of a secure internal AI assistant for employees across the organization. The assistant will provide conversational support for common workplace tasks, retrieve information from approved internal sources, assist with drafting and analysis, and help employees navigate policies, processes, and organizational knowledge. The deployment will be governed by clear security, privacy, legal, and responsible-use standards, with human oversight retained for consequential decisions and sensitive work.

The proposed initiative will establish a scalable foundation for future AI capabilities while delivering measurable near-term value. It will begin with carefully selected use cases and pilot groups, incorporate user feedback and operational learning, and expand only after the assistant demonstrates acceptable performance, security, adoption, and business impact.

## Objectives

The primary objective is to provide employees with a trusted, easy-to-use AI assistant that improves productivity while protecting organizational data and maintaining appropriate human accountability.

The initiative will pursue five specific objectives. First, it will reduce the time employees spend locating information, producing routine content, and completing repetitive knowledge-work tasks. Second, it will improve access to approved organizational knowledge by connecting the assistant to relevant policies, procedures, guidance, and other internal content. Third, it will establish enterprise standards for the secure and responsible use of AI, including data protection, access controls, transparency, monitoring, and escalation procedures. Fourth, it will create a repeatable process for identifying, evaluating, and scaling high-value AI use cases. Finally, it will build employee confidence and capability through training, communications, and practical guidance.

The assistant is not intended to make autonomous decisions on behalf of the organization, replace expert judgment, or provide unrestricted access to confidential information. Its role will be to support employees with research, drafting, summarization, translation, brainstorming, knowledge retrieval, and other approved activities, subject to the controls appropriate to each use case.

## Scope

The initial deployment will provide a centrally managed AI assistant accessible through the organization’s approved collaboration or employee portal environment. Core capabilities will include conversational question answering, document summarization, drafting and editing, meeting and content summarization, translation, structured analysis, and retrieval of information from approved internal knowledge sources.

The assistant will initially be connected only to content that has been reviewed for ownership, access permissions, quality, and suitability for AI retrieval. Integration with internal sources may include policy libraries, employee guidance, standard operating procedures, frequently asked questions, service catalogs, and selected departmental knowledge repositories. Existing identity and access-management controls will determine what information each employee is authorized to access. The assistant will not bypass source-system permissions.

The first phase will focus on low- and moderate-risk use cases such as drafting internal communications, summarizing non-sensitive documents, preparing meeting materials, locating policies, answering routine process questions, and supporting research and analysis. Higher-risk applications—including legal advice, employment decisions, financial approvals, clinical or safety decisions, security operations, and externally binding communications—will require separate review and will not be enabled through the general employee assistant without explicit approval, additional safeguards, and designated human oversight.

The program will include platform selection or configuration, security and privacy assessment, knowledge-source preparation, user experience design, pilot deployment, training, adoption support, performance monitoring, and governance. It will not initially include fully autonomous agents, unrestricted access to all organizational data, automated decisions affecting individuals, or the replacement of existing systems of record.

## Delivery Approach and Timeline

The deployment will be delivered over approximately twelve months, followed by ongoing optimization and governance.

During the first two months, the organization will establish the program foundation. This work will confirm executive sponsorship, appoint a product owner, define governance and decision rights, document priority use cases, assess available technology options, and establish baseline measures for productivity, employee experience, security, and support demand. The team will also complete an initial legal, privacy, cybersecurity, records-management, and accessibility review.

Months three and four will focus on solution design and readiness. The organization will configure or procure the assistant, define the target architecture, establish identity and access controls, implement logging and monitoring, and develop standards for prompt handling, data retention, acceptable use, and incident response. Priority internal knowledge sources will be inventoried, cleaned, structured, and prepared for retrieval. At the same time, the program will create training materials, communications, support procedures, and evaluation methods.

A controlled pilot will run during months five and six with approximately 250 to 500 employees representing a diverse set of functions, roles, technical abilities, and information needs. Pilot users will receive structured onboarding and will be asked to complete representative tasks, report errors, and provide feedback. The pilot will measure response quality, task completion time, user satisfaction, adoption, support requirements, and any privacy or security concerns. The program team will refine the assistant, improve source content, and address identified risks before expansion.

Months seven through nine will support an expanded rollout to approximately 1,500 to 2,000 employees across additional departments. The rollout will use a train-the-trainer model supported by local champions, manager briefings, office hours, and targeted communications. Use cases will be expanded selectively based on pilot evidence, and business units will be required to nominate accountable owners for any department-specific knowledge or workflows connected to the assistant.

Months ten through twelve will complete the organization-wide deployment, subject to meeting defined readiness criteria. The assistant will become available to the remaining employee population, supported by self-service learning, a centralized knowledge base, service-desk procedures, and ongoing monitoring. At the end of the first year, the organization will conduct a formal benefits review and approve a roadmap for advanced capabilities, including carefully governed workflow assistance and specialized departmental assistants.

Following the initial deployment, the program will transition into an operational product model. Performance, security, content quality, usage, and employee feedback will be reviewed regularly. New integrations and use cases will be approved through a risk-based intake process rather than enabled by default.

## Resource Requirements

The initiative will require executive sponsorship, cross-functional governance, a dedicated delivery team, technology investment, and sustained operational support.

A core program team of approximately 12 to 18 full-time equivalent staff will be appropriate during implementation. This team should include a product or program lead; solution and enterprise architects; AI or machine-learning specialists; data and knowledge engineers; cybersecurity and privacy representatives; legal and compliance advisors; user-experience and service-design specialists; change-management and communications leads; training resources; and business analysts responsible for use-case evaluation and benefits measurement. Subject-matter experts from participating departments will contribute part-time to validate content, test responses, and define acceptable use.

After organization-wide launch, approximately 6 to 10 full-time equivalent roles will be needed for ongoing operations, depending on the selected platform and the number of integrations. These roles will manage the product roadmap, platform administration, knowledge-source quality, model and response evaluation, security monitoring, user support, training, governance, and vendor relationships.

The technology environment will require an approved AI platform, enterprise identity integration, role-based access controls, secure application hosting, data-loss-prevention controls, audit logging, monitoring, analytics, and integration with selected internal knowledge repositories. The organization should favor solutions that provide strong contractual protections for organizational data, clear data-retention controls, configurable model behavior, transparent administration, accessibility support, and the ability to prevent organizational content from being used to train public models without authorization.

The program should also establish an annual operating budget covering platform licensing or consumption, implementation services, security and compliance assessments, content remediation, training, support, evaluation, and continuous improvement. The final budget will depend on platform choice, usage volume, integration complexity, and the number of specialized capabilities enabled. A contingency reserve should be included to address unforeseen data-cleanup, integration, and change-management requirements.

## Governance, Risk, and Responsible Use

The assistant will operate under an enterprise AI governance framework approved before pilot launch. A steering committee with representation from technology, security, privacy, legal, risk, human resources, communications, records management, accessibility, and major business functions will provide oversight. The committee will approve high-risk use cases, review performance and incidents, and determine whether additional capabilities are ready for release.

The organization will publish an acceptable-use policy explaining what employees may and may not submit to the assistant, how outputs should be reviewed, and when human expertise or formal business processes are required. Users will be informed that AI-generated content can be inaccurate, incomplete, biased, or misleading. The interface should provide clear guidance to verify important information and should identify the sources used for knowledge-retrieval responses wherever feasible.

Security controls will include least-privilege access, encryption, tenant isolation, secure configuration, vulnerability management, activity logging, retention controls, and monitoring for inappropriate use or attempted data exfiltration. Privacy controls will address personal information, sensitive records, employee data, data minimization, retention, and applicable regulatory requirements. The program will define procedures for reporting incorrect or harmful outputs, privacy concerns, security events, copyright issues, and inappropriate content.

Human accountability will remain mandatory for consequential decisions and external or legally binding communications. The assistant may support those activities only where the responsible professional reviews and approves the result and where the use case has received the appropriate risk assessment.

## Success Criteria

Success will be assessed through a balanced set of adoption, productivity, quality, risk, and employee-experience measures. By the end of the first year, the program should aim for at least 60 percent of employees to have access to the assistant and at least 40 percent of enabled employees to use it monthly, with sustained growth after launch. At least 70 percent of pilot and early-release users should report that the assistant saves time or improves the quality of their work.

For priority use cases, the program should demonstrate a measurable reduction in task-completion time, with an initial target of 20 to 30 percent for activities such as policy retrieval, document summarization, drafting, and routine research. Response evaluations should achieve an agreed quality threshold, such as at least 85 percent of sampled answers being judged useful and materially correct, with source attribution available for knowledge-retrieval responses. Critical errors, unauthorized disclosures, and unresolved high-severity incidents should remain at zero, and all identified incidents should be documented, investigated, and addressed within defined service levels.

Additional measures will include employee satisfaction, training completion, support-ticket volume and resolution time, content-source freshness, accessibility conformance, cost per active user, and the number and value of approved departmental use cases. Benefits should be validated through a combination of system analytics, user surveys, task-based testing, and business-unit reporting rather than relying solely on self-reported productivity.

The initiative will be considered ready for full deployment only when the pilot demonstrates acceptable security and privacy performance, reliable access controls, satisfactory response quality, effective support procedures, and positive user adoption. Continued investment will depend on evidence that the assistant is delivering measurable value while operating within the organization’s risk tolerance.

## Conclusion

Deploying an internal AI assistant across a 5,000-employee organization offers a practical opportunity to improve productivity, strengthen access to institutional knowledge, and establish a disciplined foundation for future AI adoption. The recommended phased approach balances speed with appropriate safeguards. By beginning with controlled use cases, preparing internal content, maintaining human accountability, and measuring results transparently, the organization can deliver meaningful benefits while managing the operational, legal, security, and cultural risks associated with enterprise AI.

Approval of this proposal will authorize the twelve-month implementation program, the formation of the cross-functional governance structure, the allocation of the required delivery and operating resources, and the launch of a controlled pilot as the first step toward organization-wide availability.

- Improvement in answer quality and user trust over time, supported by source attribution, feedback mechanisms, and documented correction of recurring errors.
- All production knowledge sources have designated owners, review dates, access controls, and documented quality standards.
- The platform meets agreed service-level objectives for availability, responsiveness, support response, and incident management.
- At least three high-value, repeatable use cases are documented with measured benefits and approved for continued investment.

Success will be evaluated through a combination of platform analytics, employee surveys, task-based studies, support data, business-unit metrics, quality reviews, and risk reporting. ## Conclusion

Deploying an internal AI assistant across a 5,000-employee organization represents a significant opportunity to improve productivity, strengthen access to organizational knowledge, and establish a foundation for responsible AI-enabled operations. The recommended phased approach balances speed with appropriate attention to security, privacy, content quality, employee readiness, and measurable business value.

Approval of this proposal will authorize the organization to begin the foundation phase, establish the cross-functional governance structure, complete platform and risk assessments, and develop the detailed implementation and financial plans. The core delivery team should include an AI or enterprise architect, platform and integration engineers, data and knowledge-management specialists, information-security and privacy representatives, a user-experience or service-design lead, change-management and communications support, a training lead, a business analyst, and service-desk representatives. Subject-matter experts from participating departments will be needed to validate content, define use cases, and evaluate response quality.

The technical environment will require an enterprise AI platform with contractual protections for organizational data, single sign-on, role-based access, encryption, administrative controls, audit logging, usage analytics, content filtering, and options to prevent organizational data from being used to train public models. Additional requirements will include secure connectors to approved data sources, a test environment, monitoring and evaluation tools, incident-management workflows, and reliable support coverage.

The budget will include platform licensing or consumption charges, implementation and integration services, data preparation and content remediation, security and privacy assessments, employee training, communications, change management, support operations, and ongoing administration. A contingency should be reserved for unplanned integration work, remediation of poorly structured content, additional controls, and scaling-related costs. The organization should establish a clear cost model before full deployment, including expected usage by employee population and business function.

## Governance, Risk, and Responsible Use

The assistant will operate under a formal responsible-AI policy approved before the pilot begins. The policy will define permitted and prohibited uses, requirements for human review, handling of confidential and personal information, accountability for generated content, retention and monitoring practices, accessibility expectations, and procedures for reporting incidents or harmful outputs.

All connected content sources will have an identified business owner and a defined review and refresh process. Responses will display appropriate source references where technically feasible, and users will be reminded to verify important information before relying on it. High-impact use cases will require documented risk assessment and explicit approval. The organization will maintain an inventory of AI capabilities, conduct periodic access reviews, and monitor for unauthorized data exposure, inaccurate responses, bias, misuse, and declining content quality.

The assistant will be configured to refuse or redirect requests that present unacceptable security, privacy, safety, or compliance risks. Monitoring will focus on patterns and system performance rather than unnecessary surveillance of individual employees. Employee communications will clearly explain what usage data is collected, why it is collected, and how it is governed.

## Success Criteria

The deployment will be considered successful when the assistant is available to all employees through an approved and supported access channel; complies with organizational security, privacy, accessibility, and records-management requirements; and demonstrates reliable performance across the priority use cases identified during discovery.

Adoption targets will include participation by at least 60 percent of employees within six months of organization-wide launch and regular monthly use by at least 40 percent of employees within the first year. The program should demonstrate measurable time savings for common tasks, with a target of at least 20 percent improvement for selected activities such as information retrieval, document summarization, meeting follow-up, and first-draft creation.

Quality targets should include strong user ratings for usefulness and ease of use, a material reduction in time required to locate approved internal information, and an established accuracy benchmark for each major knowledge domain. The organization should also achieve high completion rates for required training and demonstrate that reported security, privacy, and content-quality issues are investigated and resolved within defined service levels.

Business success will ultimately be assessed through a combination of quantitative and qualitative evidence: productivity improvements, reduced search and administrative effort, increased reuse of organizational knowledge, employee satisfaction, manager feedback, support trends, and documented value from priority departments. The program should have no unresolved critical security or privacy findings at the point of full deployment, and every major capability should have a named owner, documented controls, and a plan for continuous improvement.

## Conclusion

Deploying an internal AI assistant across a 5,000-employee organization represents a significant opportunity to improve productivity, strengthen access to knowledge, and establish a practical foundation for responsible enterprise AI. A phased approach will allow the organization to demonstrate value quickly while managing security, privacy, quality, adoption, and operational risks. With executive sponsorship, disciplined governance, appropriate technical investment, and sustained attention to employee needs, the assistant can become a trusted part of everyday work rather than a standalone technology experiment.

A site will have a loading dock that cannot accommodate the new chassis. A regional manager will insist that the old devices remain in service until after quarter close. Someone will discover that the configuration profile was written for an operating system version nobody deployed, while someone else will quietly reveal that the only person who knows how to fix it left three months ago. None of these problems will appear in the business case, because none of them are procurement problems.

The real work is building a system that can absorb those surprises without turning every exception into a crisis. You need inventory that reflects reality, owners who can make decisions quickly, and a transition plan that assumes people will be busy, skeptical, and occasionally wrong. The refresh succeeds when the new hardware becomes unremarkable before the old hardware becomes impossible to support.

A site manager will need a configuration nobody else needs. A vendor will quietly substitute a component that was “equivalent” until the first driver update. Someone will discover that the machines ordered for a warehouse cannot survive the warehouse, while the machines ordered for the office have been over-specified for tasks that amount to email and a browser tab left open overnight. None of these problems is individually fatal. Together, they turn a clean replacement schedule into a negotiation with every team that has ever touched a device.

The real work is in preserving continuity while changing everything underneath it. Profiles have to move, peripherals have to be tested, certificates have to follow people, and old equipment has to remain available just long enough to make the new equipment look unreliable. By the time the last asset tag is reconciled, the organization has usually learned the lesson the spreadsheet concealed: a refresh is not a purchase. It is a controlled migration with a deadline, a budget, and several hundred opportunities for someone to say, “That’s not how we use it.”

A regional office will need a different docking standard. A critical application will refuse to run on the approved image. Someone will discover that the devices assigned to the night shift spend most of their lives in a locked cabinet, while the ones assigned to field teams are exposed to weather, vibration, and the occasional improvised charging arrangement. None of these problems are especially dramatic on their own. Together, they turn a clean replacement schedule into a negotiation with every assumption the schedule was built on.

The real work is not choosing what comes next; it is deciding what cannot come with you. Old drivers, local workarounds, undocumented dependencies, and the belief that every user needs the same thing will all make a case for staying. Some of them will even have evidence. A successful refresh is less about moving inventory from one column to another than creating enough operational confidence that people are willing to let the old equipment disappear.

A regional office will discover that its preferred configuration was never approved, a finance partner will point out that the lease terms changed in a footnote, and someone will ask whether the old devices can remain in service “just a little longer.” That phrase has no operational meaning, but it has considerable political force. Suddenly the refresh is no longer a replacement program; it is a negotiation between standards, exceptions, and the calendar.

The real work is keeping those negotiations from becoming the system. You need a disposition path for every edge case, an owner for every decision, and enough slack in the schedule to absorb the surprises without making them permanent. Otherwise the fleet will age unevenly, the support burden will migrate to the most visible teams, and six months later you will be explaining why a project that was technically complete still feels unfinished.

# Project Proposal: Enterprise Internal AI Assistant Deployment

## Background

The organization’s 5,000 employees rely on a growing collection of policies, procedures, applications, documents, and subject-matter experts to complete routine work and make informed decisions. Although this information is valuable, it is distributed across collaboration platforms, intranets, shared drives, knowledge bases, and business systems. Employees often spend significant time searching for information, interpreting internal policies, drafting documents, summarizing material, and responding to recurring questions.

Recent advances in generative artificial intelligence create an opportunity to provide employees with a secure, organization-wide assistant that can help them find trusted information, create and refine content, summarize documents, analyze approved data, and complete routine knowledge-work tasks. A carefully governed internal AI assistant can improve productivity and consistency while preserving human accountability, data protection, and appropriate access controls.

This proposal recommends a phased deployment of an internal AI assistant for all employees. The assistant will be designed as a secure enterprise service that respects existing identity, permissions, retention, and information-security policies. It will augment employees rather than replace professional judgment, and its initial use cases will focus on low- and moderate-risk activities with clear opportunities for measurable productivity gains.

## Objectives

The primary objective is to make reliable AI assistance available to every employee through a consistent, secure, and easy-to-use experience. The assistant will provide conversational access to approved internal knowledge and support common tasks such as drafting emails and reports, summarizing documents and meetings, preparing first drafts, translating or reformatting content, generating ideas, and locating policies, procedures, and expertise.

The project will also establish the governance, technical controls, operating processes, and workforce capabilities required for responsible long-term use of AI. This includes implementing access controls, data-loss prevention, audit logging, usage monitoring, model-risk management, content-quality controls, and clear guidance on appropriate and prohibited uses.

A further objective is to build an evidence-based business case for expanding AI into selected departmental workflows. The initial deployment will identify high-value use cases, measure actual productivity and quality improvements, and provide a repeatable process for evaluating future AI applications.

## Proposed Solution and Scope

The project will deploy a centrally managed internal AI assistant accessible through the organization’s existing collaboration and productivity environment, with support for web and mobile access where appropriate. Employees will authenticate using the organization’s identity platform, and the assistant will enforce existing role-based permissions when retrieving or presenting internal information. It will not expose content that a user could not already access through approved systems.

The initial solution will support general enterprise use cases, including internal knowledge search, policy and procedure questions, document drafting, summarization, meeting preparation, content transformation, brainstorming, and basic assistance with approved operational tasks. The assistant will provide citations or links to source material whenever it answers questions using internal content, and it will clearly indicate when a response is generated without a verified internal source.

The first release will include a curated set of high-value knowledge sources, such as the corporate intranet, approved policy repositories, human resources guidance, information-technology support content, and selected departmental knowledge bases. Content owners will be responsible for validating source material, identifying outdated or restricted content, and establishing review cycles.

The project includes the design and implementation of the AI platform, integration with identity and access management, connection to approved knowledge sources, security and privacy review, user training, communications, support processes, and performance measurement. It also includes a controlled pilot and a phased organization-wide rollout.

The initial scope excludes autonomous actions that create financial, legal, employment, safety, or regulatory commitments; automated decisions about employees or customers; unsupervised changes to business records; and access to highly sensitive or regulated data unless a separate risk assessment and approval have been completed. These capabilities may be considered in later phases under stricter controls.

## Delivery Approach and Timeline

The deployment will take place over approximately twelve months, followed by an ongoing optimization period.

During months one and two, the project team will complete discovery and planning. This phase will confirm business priorities, identify target use cases, inventory candidate knowledge sources, assess data quality, define security and privacy requirements, select the technology platform, and establish governance. The team will also define acceptable-use policies, risk classifications, evaluation methods, support procedures, and baseline productivity measures.

During months three and four, the team will configure the platform and build the initial service. This work will include identity integration, permission enforcement, content connectors, source citation, logging, monitoring, administrative controls, and user-facing guidance. A representative set of internal content will be prepared and tested. Security, privacy, legal, accessibility, and records-management reviews will be completed before pilot launch.

During months five and six, the assistant will be piloted with approximately 300 to 500 employees from functions such as information technology, human resources, finance, operations, communications, and selected business units. Pilot participants will receive training and structured guidance, and their feedback will be used to improve response quality, content coverage, usability, and governance. The team will compare results against baseline measures and address critical defects before broader deployment.

During months seven through nine, the assistant will expand to approximately 1,500 employees across the organization. Additional knowledge sources and departmental use cases will be introduced based on pilot results. Champions in each participating function will support adoption, collect feedback, and help identify content gaps and emerging risks.

During months ten through twelve, the service will be rolled out to the remaining employees in staged waves. Organization-wide communications, training, office hours, and support resources will accompany the rollout. At the end of this phase, the project team will complete a formal benefits review, document lessons learned, and recommend the next set of departmental integrations and higher-value use cases.

After the initial twelve-month deployment, the assistant will transition to steady-state operations. The organization will maintain a quarterly review cycle covering usage, quality, security events, content freshness, user feedback, and financial performance.

## Resource Requirements

The project will require a cross-functional team with authority to make timely decisions about technology, risk, content, and adoption. A core team of approximately 12 to 16 full-time equivalent staff, supplemented by part-time subject-matter experts, is recommended during implementation.

Key roles will include an executive sponsor, a product owner, a program manager, an enterprise architect, AI and application engineers, data and knowledge engineers, an information-security lead, a privacy and legal representative, an identity and access-management specialist, content owners, user-experience and accessibility specialists, a change-management lead, trainers, communications staff, and service-desk representatives. Each participating business function should appoint a part-time AI champion and content steward.

The project will require funding for platform licensing or model consumption, secure hosting and integration, data preparation, monitoring and evaluation tools, implementation services where needed, training and communications, and ongoing support. A preliminary first-year estimate is $1.5 million to $2.5 million, depending on the selected platform, licensing model, integration complexity, usage volume, and the extent of external implementation support. The budget should include a contingency for additional data remediation, security controls, and adoption activities.

The organization will also need executive sponsorship, timely participation from legal, privacy, security, human resources, records management, procurement, and employee-relations functions, and access to subject-matter experts who can validate content and define acceptable use. The assistant’s effectiveness will depend heavily on the quality, structure, ownership, and maintenance of the information it is permitted to use.

## Governance, Risk, and Responsible Use

The assistant will operate under a formal governance framework approved before pilot launch. The framework will define permitted, restricted, and prohibited uses; responsibilities for users and content owners; review and escalation procedures; data-handling requirements; monitoring and audit practices; and criteria for approving new integrations.

Users will be informed that AI-generated content may be inaccurate, incomplete, or out of date and must be reviewed before use. The assistant will not be presented as an authoritative decision-maker. Responses involving sensitive subjects will include appropriate guidance to consult a qualified human expert or official source. High-risk use cases will require additional legal, privacy, security, and business approval.

Technical safeguards will include single sign-on, role-based access, encryption, tenant and data isolation, prompt and response logging subject to privacy requirements, malware and data-loss protections, administrative controls, content filtering, abuse monitoring, and incident-response procedures. The organization will establish a process for reporting incorrect, unsafe, biased, or inappropriate responses and will use those reports to improve the service.

## Success Criteria

The project will be considered successful when the assistant is securely available to all employees, has completed the required governance and assurance reviews, and demonstrates sustained value in real-world work. Within six months of organization-wide rollout, the target is for at least 80 percent of employees to activate the service and at least 60 percent to use it monthly, with adoption distributed across business functions rather than concentrated in a small group of early adopters.

For employees who use the assistant regularly, the organization will target an average reduction of at least 20 percent in the time required for selected tasks such as information retrieval, document drafting, summarization, and routine internal inquiries. At least three high-volume use cases should demonstrate measurable productivity or service-quality improvement, and employee surveys should show that at least 70 percent of active users consider the assistant useful and easy to use.

Quality and trust will be measured through response evaluations, source-citation rates, user feedback, and human review. The target is for at least 90 percent of evaluated responses in approved knowledge-search scenarios to be materially accurate and appropriately sourced, with clear escalation paths for the remaining cases. The project must also achieve zero critical security or privacy incidents attributable to the deployment and maintain compliance with applicable information-security, privacy, records-management, accessibility, and employment requirements.

Operationally, the service should meet agreed availability and support targets, with a documented ownership model and predictable operating costs. A formal benefits review will compare measured productivity gains, adoption, support demand, risk events, and total cost of ownership against the original business case. The results will determine whether the organization should expand the assistant’s access to additional data sources, automate selected workflows, or invest in specialized departmental AI solutions.

## Conclusion

Deploying an internal AI assistant across a 5,000-employee organization is a strategic productivity and capability initiative, not simply a software installation. Success will depend on combining a secure technical foundation with reliable internal content, clear governance, employee training, and disciplined measurement. A phased twelve-month implementation will allow the organization to demonstrate value quickly while managing risk, learning from employee experience, and building the operating model required for responsible enterprise-wide AI adoption.

Recent advances in generative artificial intelligence provide an opportunity to improve how employees access knowledge and complete everyday work. An internal AI assistant could provide a secure, conversational interface for finding approved information, summarizing documents, drafting communications, explaining procedures, and supporting selected business workflows. Deployed responsibly, the assistant would augment employees rather than replace them, improving productivity while preserving human accountability for decisions and actions.

This proposal recommends a phased deployment of an internal AI assistant for the organization. The solution would be accessible through approved enterprise channels, grounded in organizational data, governed according to security and privacy requirements, and introduced through controlled pilots before broader availability.

## Objectives

The primary objective is to provide employees with a trusted, secure, and easy-to-use AI assistant that reduces the time required to find information and complete common knowledge-work tasks.

The initiative will pursue five related objectives. First, it will improve access to authoritative organizational knowledge by allowing employees to ask questions in natural language and receive responses that cite approved source materials. Second, it will increase productivity by supporting activities such as drafting, summarization, translation, meeting preparation, information extraction, and process navigation. Third, it will reduce avoidable demand on support functions by addressing common questions about policies, procedures, technology, human resources, finance, and other internal services. Fourth, it will establish an enterprise framework for responsible AI use, including access controls, data protection, monitoring, human oversight, and acceptable-use standards. Finally, it will create a scalable foundation for future AI-enabled workflows and integrations.

The assistant will be designed to complement existing systems and expertise. It will not be positioned as an autonomous decision-maker, a substitute for professional judgment, or an unrestricted interface to sensitive organizational data.

## Scope

The initial solution will provide a secure conversational assistant available through the organization’s approved collaboration or intranet environment. It will support general question answering over approved internal content, with responses grounded in indexed organizational documents and links to source material where available. Users will be authenticated through the organization’s identity platform, and access to content will respect existing permissions wherever technically feasible.

Initial use cases will include policy and procedure navigation, employee-service questions, information retrieval, document summarization, drafting of routine communications, meeting preparation, creation of first drafts for reports and presentations, and conversion of unstructured information into structured summaries or action items. Selected integrations may be introduced during the pilot or subsequent releases, including links to the knowledge base, service desk, document repositories, collaboration platforms, and approved business applications.

The program will include data classification, content readiness assessment, prompt and response monitoring, user training, support processes, and a governance model covering privacy, security, legal review, records management, accessibility, and responsible use. It will also establish a process for evaluating new use cases and approving future integrations.

The initial release will exclude fully autonomous actions that create financial, legal, employment, safety, or external commitments without human review. The assistant will not make employment decisions, provide unverified legal or regulatory advice, modify authoritative records without approval, or expose information beyond a user’s authorized access. Highly sensitive content, including certain personal, confidential, regulated, or security-critical data, will remain excluded until appropriate controls have been validated.

## Delivery Approach and Timeline

The deployment will be completed over approximately nine months, followed by an ongoing optimization period.

During the first month, the project team will confirm executive sponsorship, finalize the business case, establish governance, define priority use cases, and document security, privacy, legal, accessibility, and procurement requirements. The team will also identify initial data sources and assess their quality, ownership, permissions, and suitability for use with an AI system.

Months two and three will focus on solution design and preparation. This phase will include selecting or confirming the technology platform, configuring identity and access controls, establishing the target architecture, preparing approved content, defining evaluation standards, and developing the initial assistant experience. The team will create policies for acceptable use, human review, incident reporting, data retention, and model or prompt changes. A representative test environment will be established to evaluate answer quality, security, bias, privacy, and resilience against misuse.

Months four and five will comprise a controlled pilot involving approximately 300 to 500 employees from a representative set of functions. Pilot users will receive training and clear guidance on appropriate use. The project team will monitor adoption, response quality, user feedback, security events, and operational impact. Pilot use cases will be limited to approved content and low-risk tasks while the team addresses defects and improves the underlying knowledge sources.

Months six and seven will support a broader release to approximately 1,500 employees across additional departments. New content sources and use cases will be added only after review. The organization will launch a communications and enablement campaign, establish a support model, and publish practical examples of effective and responsible use. Feedback from this release will inform final configuration, service levels, and the organization-wide rollout plan.

Months eight and nine will be dedicated to enterprise deployment for the remaining employees, subject to meeting the agreed readiness criteria. This phase will include final security and operational validation, completion of training resources, onboarding of business and technical support teams, and transition from project delivery to steady-state ownership. Following deployment, the assistant will enter an optimization cycle focused on improving content quality, expanding approved integrations, refining evaluation methods, and measuring business outcomes.

## Resource Requirements

The initiative will require an executive sponsor and a cross-functional delivery team. Core staffing should include a program manager, product owner, enterprise architect, AI or machine-learning engineer, data and knowledge engineers, security architect, privacy and legal representatives, user-experience designer, change-management lead, training and communications specialists, and business representatives from the pilot functions. Subject-matter experts will be needed to validate high-value content and define authoritative answers for priority processes.

A reasonable initial staffing model is approximately 10 to 14 full-time equivalent resources during design and pilot delivery, supplemented by part-time participation from information owners, legal and compliance teams, service-desk personnel, and departmental champions. The team should also establish an AI governance group with representatives from technology, security, privacy, legal, records management, human resources, risk, accessibility, and key business functions.

The technology environment will require an approved AI platform or model service, enterprise identity integration, secure data connectors, document indexing and retrieval capabilities, monitoring and analytics, content-management tooling, and a test environment isolated from production where appropriate. The organization will need to budget for platform licensing, model usage, integration work, data preparation, security testing, training, support, and ongoing content maintenance. An indicative first-year investment is expected to fall in the range of $1.5 million to $3 million, depending on the selected platform, number of integrations, licensing model, and level of custom development.

Business units will be responsible for identifying authoritative content owners, correcting obsolete or conflicting information, reviewing proposed use cases, and assigning employees to participate in pilots and training. The service will require an ongoing operating model after launch, including a product owner, platform administration, knowledge management, model and response evaluation, user support, governance reviews, and continuous improvement.

## Governance, Risk, and Change Management

The assistant will operate under a formal responsible-AI framework. Every approved use case will have a defined business owner, data classification, risk rating, human-review requirement, and evaluation method. Access will be based on organizational identity and existing permissions. Prompts and responses will be handled according to approved data-protection standards, and the organization will not use employee interactions for model training without explicit authorization and appropriate safeguards.

Responses will include clear guidance that users remain responsible for reviewing outputs before relying on them. Where feasible, answers will identify source documents, document dates, and relevant owners. High-risk topics will be routed to established human channels rather than answered automatically. Monitoring will detect potential data leakage, harmful content, misuse, poor-quality responses, and significant changes in performance. A documented incident process will define how issues are reported, investigated, remediated, and communicated.

Adoption will be supported through role-based training, short demonstrations, practical guidance, manager briefings, frequently asked questions, and a network of departmental champions. Communications will emphasize the assistant’s benefits and limitations, including the need to protect confidential information, verify outputs, and follow existing policies.

## Success Criteria

The deployment will be considered successful when the assistant is available to the organization’s employees through approved channels, operates within documented security and governance controls, and demonstrates measurable value in priority use cases.

By the end of the first year, the program should achieve at least 60 percent registration among eligible employees and 40 percent monthly active usage, with higher adoption in pilot and targeted business areas. At least 70 percent of active users should report that the assistant reduces the time required to find information or complete routine tasks. For selected use cases, the organization should demonstrate a 20 percent or greater reduction in time spent on information retrieval, drafting, or routine service inquiries.

The assistant should achieve a minimum of 85 percent acceptable-response quality in evaluated priority scenarios, with source attribution available for at least 90 percent of knowledge-based responses where authoritative sources exist. Critical security or privacy incidents attributable to the service should be zero, and all identified high-severity defects should have documented remediation plans and owners. Support teams should also report a measurable reduction in repetitive inquiries for the functions included in the pilot.

Success will be reviewed at the end of the pilot, at broader release, and six months after enterprise deployment. Continued investment will be based not only on usage, but also on measurable productivity gains, employee experience, content quality, risk performance, and the ability to expand the assistant responsibly into additional business processes.

Any critical incident will trigger immediate investigation and, where necessary, suspension of the affected capability.

The program will ultimately be judged not only by usage, but by whether it creates a trusted and sustainable internal capability. Initial capabilities will focus on information retrieval, writing assistance, summarization, and workflow guidance, with more advanced integrations introduced after the platform has demonstrated reliability and appropriate controls.

## Objectives

The primary objective is to provide employees with a trusted, easy-to-use AI assistant that improves productivity while protecting confidential information and maintaining human accountability.

The project will pursue five specific objectives. First, it will make approved organizational knowledge easier to discover by allowing employees to ask questions in natural language and receive answers grounded in authoritative internal sources. Second, it will reduce time spent on routine knowledge work, including drafting, summarizing, formatting, and preparing materials. Third, it will improve consistency by directing employees to current policies, standard procedures, templates, and approved guidance. Fourth, it will establish a durable governance model covering privacy, security, access control, records management, acceptable use, model evaluation, and ongoing oversight. Finally, it will create a scalable foundation for future AI-enabled workflows, including carefully governed connections to selected business systems.

The assistant will be positioned as a support tool. Employees will remain responsible for reviewing outputs, applying professional judgment, and following established approval processes. The system will not independently make employment, financial, legal, safety, or other high-impact decisions.

## Scope

The initial solution will be available through the organization’s approved collaboration or employee portal and will use single sign-on and existing role-based access controls. It will provide conversational search across selected internal sources, including policies, procedures, employee handbooks, process documentation, knowledge bases, templates, and other approved content repositories. Responses will include links or citations to source material wherever feasible so that employees can verify information.

The assistant will support common productivity tasks such as summarizing documents, drafting emails and internal communications, rewriting content for clarity or tone, extracting action items, generating meeting agendas, creating first drafts of presentations or reports, and translating or simplifying approved business content. It will also provide guided answers to common HR, IT, procurement, facilities, and operational questions, while routing users to human support or formal workflows when a request requires authorization, case handling, or expert judgment.

The project includes data-source assessment and preparation, identity and access integration, security and privacy design, platform configuration, prompt and response safeguards, user training, communications, pilot testing, usage analytics, and post-launch support. It also includes the creation of governance processes for content ownership, incident reporting, model evaluation, access reviews, and changes to the assistant’s capabilities.

The initial scope excludes autonomous decision-making, unrestricted access to all organizational data, unsupervised execution of transactions, and use of sensitive information outside approved business purposes. Integrations with systems of record will be limited during the first release and introduced only after technical, legal, security, and business-owner approval. Personal data, regulated information, privileged legal material, and highly confidential business information will be subject to additional controls and may be excluded from the initial knowledge base.

## Delivery Approach and Timeline

The proposed implementation will take approximately nine months from approval to full organizational rollout, followed by continuous improvement.

During the first month, the project team will establish the program charter, confirm executive sponsorship, define use cases, identify business owners, assess current data and technology environments, and establish the initial risk classification. The team will also select the preferred technology approach, whether through an enterprise AI platform, a managed model service, or a combination of approved technologies.

Months two and three will focus on solution design and preparation. This phase will include architecture, identity and access design, data-source inventories, content-quality assessment, security and privacy reviews, retention requirements, acceptable-use policies, and evaluation standards. Priority content will be cleaned, classified, permissioned, and prepared for retrieval. The organization will also define escalation paths for inaccurate, unsafe, or inappropriate responses.

During months four and five, the team will configure the platform and build the minimum viable assistant. Initial capabilities will include authenticated conversational access to selected internal content, citations to source materials, general drafting and summarization, feedback collection, usage monitoring, and administrative controls. Technical testing will assess response quality, data leakage risk, access-control enforcement, prompt injection, inappropriate content, availability, and performance.

Months six and seven will comprise a controlled pilot involving approximately 300 to 500 employees from representative functions, including corporate services, operations, technology, finance, human resources, and other knowledge-intensive teams. Pilot participants will receive training and clear guidance on appropriate use. Their feedback will be used to improve content, prompts, user experience, safeguards, and support procedures. The pilot will also establish a baseline for productivity, satisfaction, accuracy, and support impact.

During month eight, the organization will prepare for scale. This work will include finalizing governance approvals, expanding the knowledge base, completing accessibility and usability testing, training managers and support teams, publishing user guidance, and preparing a phased communications campaign. Critical issues identified during the pilot will be resolved before broader access is granted.

In month nine, the assistant will be rolled out to the remaining employees in stages, with monitoring after each deployment wave. Adoption, system performance, response quality, security events, and support demand will be reviewed throughout the rollout. At the end of the initial deployment, the program will transition into an operational service with quarterly governance reviews and a prioritized roadmap for additional integrations and capabilities.

## Resource Requirements

The program will require executive sponsorship from a senior leader with authority across business, technology, risk, and support functions. A steering committee should include representatives from information technology, information security, privacy, legal, human resources, compliance, communications, records management, accessibility, and major business divisions.

A core delivery team of approximately 10 to 14 full-time equivalent staff is recommended during implementation. This team should include a program manager; product owner; enterprise or solution architect; AI or machine-learning engineer; data and knowledge engineer; two to three application or integration engineers; security and privacy specialists; a user-experience or service-design lead; a change-management and training lead; and a business analyst or measurement lead. Subject-matter experts and content owners from participating departments will contribute part-time to validate sources, define use cases, and approve responses and workflows.

The technology environment will require an approved enterprise AI platform or model provider, secure hosting, encryption in transit and at rest, identity federation, role-based access controls, audit logging, monitoring, content-filtering and data-loss-prevention capabilities, and integration with selected document and collaboration systems. The solution should support model and prompt versioning, evaluation datasets, usage analytics, administrative configuration, and the ability to disable or restrict capabilities when necessary.

The organization should establish an implementation and operating budget covering licensing or model usage, integration and engineering, data preparation, security testing, training, communications, accessibility, support, and ongoing governance. A contingency should be included for additional content remediation, capacity, and remediation of security or quality issues identified during the pilot. Ongoing operating costs will include platform consumption, service administration, monitoring, model evaluation, content maintenance, user support, and periodic independent reviews.

Training will be delivered through short mandatory awareness materials for all employees, role-based instruction for managers and support teams, and practical workshops for high-use departments. Training will emphasize appropriate use, verification of outputs, confidentiality, records obligations, and the requirement to follow existing approval processes.

## Governance and Risk Management

The assistant will operate under a formal AI governance framework approved before the pilot begins. Every connected data source will have an accountable owner, defined access rules, a review schedule, and a documented business purpose. The assistant will inherit or enforce source-system permissions so that users cannot retrieve content they are not otherwise authorized to access.

The program will maintain a risk register and conduct privacy, security, accessibility, and legal reviews before each major release. Responses will be monitored for accuracy, unsupported claims, bias, inappropriate disclosure, and unsafe recommendations. Users will be able to provide feedback and report problems directly from the assistant interface. Significant incidents will be investigated under established security and operational procedures, with the ability to restrict content sources or suspend features when required.

The assistant will clearly communicate that generated responses may be incomplete or incorrect. High-impact or regulated activities will require human review and, where appropriate, use of existing systems and approval channels rather than conversational automation. Content owners will be responsible for maintaining the accuracy and currency of indexed information.

## Success Criteria

The project will be considered successful when the assistant is available to all employees through approved channels, operates within established security and privacy controls, and demonstrates measurable value in everyday work.

Within six months of full rollout, the organization should target adoption by at least 60 percent of employees, with at least 40 percent using the assistant monthly. At least 70 percent of active users should report that the assistant helps them complete work more efficiently, and user satisfaction should reach an average rating of at least 4 out of 5. For priority use cases, the assistant should achieve a grounded-answer accuracy rate of at least 85 percent, with responses linked to authoritative sources wherever applicable.

The program should also demonstrate a measurable reduction in time spent locating information and completing selected routine tasks, with a target of 20 percent or more for participating use cases. Support functions should identify reductions in repetitive inquiries or improved first-response performance, while business teams should document representative examples of time saved and quality improved.

No material unauthorized disclosure of confidential information should occur. All critical security, privacy, and accessibility findings identified during testing must be resolved or formally accepted before general availability. The organization should maintain complete auditability of administrative actions, connected data sources, major configuration changes, and reported incidents.

Finally, success will be measured by the organization’s ability to operate and improve the assistant sustainably. This includes active participation by content owners, regular governance reviews, reliable support processes, a documented release roadmap, and a clear process for approving new data sources, integrations, and higher-risk capabilities. By meeting these criteria, the organization will establish not only a useful employee service but also a responsible foundation for broader adoption of artificial intelligence.

The real work is less about replacing machines than preserving all the invisible agreements attached to them. By the time the last box is opened, the refresh has become an exercise in institutional memory, conducted by whoever happens to remember why the old thing was still there.

None of these issues will appear in the asset database, because the asset database records what was purchased, not what people quietly depend on.

The real work is not moving users from one box to another; it is finding the invisible agreements that accumulated around the old fleet.
