None of these are difficult problems in isolation. Together, they become the schedule.

The real work is keeping the exceptions from becoming the process. You need a clean path for the ordinary cases, a short list of decisions that only humans can make, and enough slack to absorb the things nobody could have known in advance. The teams that finish well are not the ones with the most impressive rollout plan. They are the ones that know where the plan stops being useful, and have already decided what happens next.

# Proposal: Deployment of an Internal AI Assistant Across the Organization

## Background

The organization’s 5,000 employees rely on a wide range of systems, documents, policies, applications, and subject-matter experts to complete routine work and make informed decisions. Although this information is valuable, it is often dispersed across intranet pages, shared drives, collaboration platforms, knowledge bases, and business applications. Employees spend significant time searching for information, interpreting internal policies, drafting routine communications, summarizing documents, and repeating work that has already been completed elsewhere in the organization.

Recent advances in enterprise artificial intelligence create an opportunity to improve this experience through a secure internal AI assistant. The assistant would provide employees with a single, natural-language interface for finding approved internal information, summarizing content, drafting and transforming text, and completing selected low-risk tasks. It would operate within the organization’s existing identity, access, security, and governance frameworks, ensuring that users receive only the information they are authorized to access.

This proposal recommends a phased deployment of an internal AI assistant to all 5,000 employees, beginning with a controlled pilot and expanding through measured stages. The program will prioritize practical business value, responsible use, data protection, transparency, and long-term operational sustainability.

## Objectives

The primary objective is to give employees a trusted and easy-to-use AI capability that improves productivity without compromising confidentiality, security, compliance, or human accountability. The assistant will reduce the time required to locate and understand organizational information, support the creation of routine business content, and help employees complete common tasks more efficiently.

The program will pursue five specific outcomes. First, it will provide reliable conversational access to approved internal knowledge, including policies, procedures, operating manuals, product information, and organizational guidance. Second, it will assist with common productivity activities such as summarizing documents, preparing meeting notes, drafting emails, creating first drafts of reports, and translating or reformatting content. Third, it will support selected workflows through integrations with collaboration tools, document repositories, service-management systems, and other approved enterprise applications. Fourth, it will establish a secure and governed foundation for future AI use cases. Finally, it will build employee confidence and capability through training, clear usage guidance, and transparent communication about the assistant’s limitations.

## Scope

The initial deployment will include a secure, enterprise-managed AI assistant accessible through the organization’s standard collaboration environment and web portal. Employees will authenticate using existing single sign-on, and the assistant will enforce current identity and access permissions when retrieving or referencing internal content. Responses will include citations or links to source material where technically feasible so that employees can verify information and consult the authoritative record.

The first release will focus on low- and medium-risk use cases with broad applicability across departments. These will include enterprise search and question answering over approved internal content; summarization of documents, meetings, and correspondence; drafting and editing of internal communications; creation of outlines, briefing materials, and first drafts; extraction of action items and key themes; and assistance with standard operating procedures and service requests. The program will also evaluate integrations with platforms such as Microsoft Teams or Slack, the intranet, document-management systems, knowledge bases, and service-management tools.

The assistant will not make final decisions on behalf of the organization, approve transactions, determine employment outcomes, provide unsupervised legal or medical advice, or independently execute high-impact actions. Any workflow automation introduced after the initial launch will require explicit authorization, appropriate controls, auditability, and human review. Sensitive use cases involving personal data, regulated information, confidential transactions, or material business decisions will be subject to additional assessment before inclusion.

The project includes platform selection or configuration, data and content assessment, security and privacy review, identity and access integration, user experience design, pilot deployment, employee training, support procedures, usage monitoring, and post-launch improvement. It also includes the development of responsible-use policies, an AI governance model, and a process for approving future use cases.

## Delivery Approach and Timeline

The program will be delivered over approximately twelve months, followed by an ongoing optimization phase.

During months one and two, the project team will establish the business case, governance model, security and privacy requirements, technical architecture, and baseline measures. Representatives from business units will identify priority use cases and assess the quality, ownership, sensitivity, and accessibility of relevant internal content. The team will also define acceptable-use standards, escalation procedures, retention requirements, and criteria for evaluating AI-generated responses.

During months three and four, the organization will configure the selected AI platform and establish the initial knowledge architecture. This phase will include integration with identity and access-management systems, approved content repositories, collaboration tools, and logging and monitoring services. A representative set of high-value content will be prepared for use, with outdated, duplicative, or improperly classified information removed or corrected. The team will conduct security testing, privacy assessment, prompt and response testing, and accessibility reviews.

During months five and six, a pilot will be conducted with approximately 300 to 500 employees drawn from a representative selection of departments, job roles, and technical environments. Pilot participants will receive training and structured guidance on appropriate use. Their feedback will be used to evaluate response quality, usefulness, ease of use, access controls, system performance, and potential risks. The pilot will also establish a realistic understanding of the types of questions employees ask and the content gaps that limit answer quality.

During months seven and eight, the project team will address pilot findings, improve content and retrieval quality, refine policies and support processes, and complete additional integrations. Business units will validate priority use cases and nominate local champions who can support adoption. The organization will also finalize communications, training materials, help-desk procedures, and performance dashboards for the broader rollout.

During months nine and ten, the assistant will be deployed in stages to the remaining employee population. Rollout waves will be sequenced to manage system capacity, support demand, and organizational readiness. Each wave will include clear communication, short mandatory orientation material, practical examples, and guidance on protecting confidential information. Departments with specialized or higher-risk requirements will receive additional review before access to expanded capabilities is enabled.

During months eleven and twelve, the organization will evaluate the first full-scale operating period, address outstanding issues, and establish the long-term operating model. This phase will include a formal benefits assessment, review of incidents and policy exceptions, prioritization of new integrations, and a decision on whether to expand the assistant into additional workflow and automation use cases.

## Resource Requirements

The implementation will require a cross-functional team of approximately 12 to 15 full-time-equivalent resources during the first year. The core team should include an executive sponsor, a program or product manager, an enterprise architect, an AI or machine-learning lead, a data and knowledge-management lead, security and privacy specialists, an identity and access-management engineer, integration engineers, a user-experience or service-design lead, a change-management and communications lead, a training lead, and representatives from legal, compliance, records management, accessibility, and internal audit.

Each participating business unit should appoint a product representative or subject-matter expert to identify use cases, validate content, participate in testing, and communicate with employees. A network of departmental champions will provide practical support during rollout and help surface improvement opportunities. The service desk and operations teams will require training and documented procedures for handling access issues, incorrect responses, suspected data exposure, and other incidents.

The technical environment will require an enterprise AI platform or model service with contractual protections for organizational data, administrative controls, usage monitoring, and the ability to prevent organizational content from being used to train public models without authorization. Additional requirements include single sign-on, role-based access controls, encryption in transit and at rest, audit logging, content filtering, data-loss-prevention controls, secure integration interfaces, performance monitoring, and disaster-recovery provisions. The program will also require funding for licensing or consumption-based model costs, integration and implementation services, content remediation, training, communications, and ongoing support.

Following implementation, the assistant should be supported by a permanent operating team of approximately six to eight full-time-equivalent resources, supplemented by part-time participation from security, privacy, legal, knowledge-management, and business-unit representatives. This team will manage platform operations, content quality, model and prompt changes, governance, incident response, user support, performance reporting, and continuous improvement.

## Governance, Risk, and Responsible Use

The assistant will be governed as an enterprise service rather than as an experimental application. An AI governance committee will oversee use-case approval, risk classification, data requirements, vendor management, policy exceptions, and periodic performance reviews. All approved use cases will have a named business owner responsible for content accuracy, user outcomes, and ongoing review.

Employees will be informed that the assistant can produce inaccurate, incomplete, outdated, or misleading responses. Training will emphasize that AI-generated content must be reviewed before it is shared, relied upon, or used in a business decision. The assistant will provide clear guidance on prohibited inputs and will be configured to limit access to sensitive information according to existing permissions. High-impact decisions will remain subject to human judgment and established organizational processes.

The organization will monitor for unauthorized access, inappropriate use, biased or harmful outputs, inaccurate responses, system outages, and material changes in model behavior. Employees will have a clear method for reporting problems, and incidents involving confidential information or significant business impact will be escalated under existing security and compliance procedures.

## Success Criteria

The program will be considered successful when the assistant is available to all 5,000 employees, operates within approved security and privacy controls, and demonstrates measurable value in daily work. Within six months of full rollout, the target is for at least 60 percent of employees to have used the assistant and for at least 35 percent to use it monthly. At least 75 percent of active users should report that the assistant helps them complete selected tasks faster or with less effort.

For priority use cases, the assistant should achieve a user-rated helpfulness score of at least 80 percent, with source-linked answers judged accurate or appropriately qualified in at least 90 percent of sampled evaluations. The organization should achieve a measurable reduction in time spent searching for internal information and preparing routine documents, with a target of at least 20 percent improvement in the pilot’s selected workflows. Support volume, access failures, and response latency should remain within agreed service levels, and all identified security or privacy incidents should be investigated and resolved through documented procedures.

Success will also be measured by the strength of the operating foundation. The organization should have an approved AI-use policy, a functioning governance committee, named owners for priority knowledge sources, trained support staff, a repeatable process for approving new use cases, and regular reporting on adoption, value, content quality, and risk. The first year will be treated as the establishment of a sustainable capability, not merely the launch of a new software product.

## Conclusion

Deploying an internal AI assistant across the organization will provide employees with faster access to knowledge, practical support for routine work, and a controlled foundation for broader AI adoption. A phased implementation will allow the organization to demonstrate value early, address security and content risks before broad release, and adapt the service to real employee needs. With appropriate governance, investment, training, and measurement, the assistant can become a trusted enterprise capability that improves productivity while preserving human accountability and organizational control.

# Project Proposal: Enterprise Internal AI Assistant Deployment

## Background

The organization’s 5,000 employees manage increasing volumes of information across documents, policies, email, collaboration platforms, business applications, and operational systems. Employees frequently spend substantial time searching for information, preparing routine communications, summarizing material, interpreting internal policies, and completing repetitive administrative work. Information is often distributed across departments and systems, making it difficult to locate authoritative answers quickly and consistently.

Recent advances in generative artificial intelligence provide an opportunity to improve how employees access knowledge and complete everyday work. An internal AI assistant can provide conversational access to approved organizational information, assist with drafting and summarization, help employees navigate policies and procedures, and support selected business workflows. This proposal recommends a phased deployment of a secure, enterprise-grade internal AI assistant for the organization’s 5,000 employees. ## Objectives

The primary objective is to provide employees with a trusted, easy-to-use AI assistant that helps them find information and complete routine work more efficiently. The assistant will be accessible through approved organizational channels and will use enterprise content only when the user has permission to access that content.

The project will pursue five related objectives. First, it will improve employee access to authoritative internal knowledge by enabling natural-language search across approved policies, procedures, guidance, and other business content. Second, it will reduce the time required for common tasks such as drafting, summarizing, preparing meeting materials, analyzing non-sensitive information, and creating first drafts of routine communications. Third, it will provide a consistent and governed platform for future AI use cases rather than allowing fragmented or unmanaged adoption of consumer tools. Fourth, it will establish clear standards for responsible AI use, including privacy, security, transparency, human review, records management, and acceptable-use requirements. Finally, it will create a scalable foundation for integrating the assistant with selected business systems and workflows over time.

The assistant will support employees rather than replace professional judgment or decision-making. It will be positioned as a productivity and knowledge-access tool, with human review required for consequential, external, legal, financial, personnel, safety, or otherwise sensitive decisions.

## Scope

The initial deployment will include a secure conversational interface available to all employees through the organization’s existing identity and collaboration environment. The assistant will support question answering over approved internal content, document summarization, drafting and rewriting, meeting and discussion summaries, idea generation, translation where appropriate, and guided access to internal policies and procedures.

The platform will integrate with selected enterprise content repositories, collaboration tools, and knowledge-management systems. Initial integrations will focus on high-value and relatively well-governed sources, such as the intranet, employee handbook, approved policy libraries, service-management knowledge bases, information-security guidance, human-resources materials, and selected departmental repositories. Content will remain subject to existing access permissions. The assistant will not provide information that the requesting employee could not otherwise access.

The project will also establish a controlled process for introducing workflow capabilities. During the initial release, these capabilities may include creating service-desk requests, locating forms, initiating approved internal processes, or generating structured summaries for review. Any action that changes a business record, sends an external communication, approves a transaction, or affects an employee or customer will require explicit user confirmation and, where applicable, a separate human approval.

The project includes platform selection or configuration, security architecture, data integration, content preparation, user-experience design, testing, pilot deployment, training, communications, support, governance, and post-launch measurement. It also includes the creation of policies covering acceptable use, data handling, human oversight, incident reporting, model limitations, and content ownership.

The initial scope excludes fully autonomous decision-making, unsupervised external communications, automated employment decisions, unrestricted access to confidential or regulated data, and use cases where an incorrect response could create unacceptable legal, safety, financial, or operational risk. These areas may be considered later through separate approval processes once the organization has established sufficient controls and evidence.

## Delivery Approach and Timeline

The deployment will be completed through a phased, approximately twelve-month program beginning upon executive approval and funding.

During the first two months, the project team will conduct discovery and establish the program foundation. This phase will confirm priority use cases, identify content and systems for the initial release, assess data quality, document security and privacy requirements, and define baseline measures for productivity, user satisfaction, and operational performance. The team will also select the preferred technology approach, whether through an approved enterprise AI platform, a managed model service, or a private deployment that meets organizational requirements.

Months three and four will focus on solution design and governance. The organization will finalize the target architecture, identity and access model, data-loss-prevention controls, logging and monitoring approach, retention requirements, and model-risk controls. A cross-functional AI governance group will approve the initial use cases and establish a process for reviewing future applications. During this phase, the team will prepare priority content, resolve ownership issues, and define standards for content freshness, source attribution, and response quality.

Months five through seven will cover configuration, integration, and controlled testing. The assistant will be connected to the initial enterprise content sources and collaboration channels. The project team will conduct functional testing, security testing, privacy reviews, prompt-injection testing, access-control validation, performance testing, and user-acceptance testing. A pilot group of approximately 300 to 500 employees will be selected to represent major functions, levels, locations, and technical proficiency. Pilot participants will receive training and clear guidance on appropriate use and will provide structured feedback.

Months eight and nine will focus on pilot evaluation and limited expansion. The team will analyze adoption, response quality, task completion time, user satisfaction, support requests, security events, and instances of inaccurate or inappropriate output. Improvements will be made to prompts, retrieval configuration, content structure, user guidance, and support processes. If the pilot meets the agreed readiness thresholds, the assistant will be expanded to additional departments in waves.

Months ten through twelve will complete the organization-wide rollout. Deployment will occur in manageable groups rather than through a single unrestricted release. Each wave will include communications, manager briefings, employee training, access to support resources, and a review of department-specific content and use cases. At the end of the rollout, the project will transition from implementation to a permanent product and service-management model, with a regular process for evaluating new capabilities and retiring low-value or unsafe uses.

## Resource Requirements

The program will require executive sponsorship, dedicated product ownership, and participation from technology, security, privacy, legal, compliance, records management, human resources, communications, and representative business units. A core team of approximately eight to twelve full-time equivalent staff, supplemented by part-time subject-matter experts and departmental representatives, is expected to be sufficient for the initial deployment. Additional capacity may be required for complex integrations, data remediation, or regulated use cases.

The technology environment will require an approved large-language-model capability, secure retrieval and indexing services, enterprise identity integration, role-based access controls, encryption, audit logging, monitoring, content-management connectors, and administrative controls for configuration and usage analytics. The selected platform must support data isolation, appropriate contractual protections, configurable retention, model and prompt monitoring, and assurance that organizational data will not be used to train a public model without explicit authorization.

Funding will be required for platform licensing or cloud consumption, implementation services, integration work, security and privacy assessment, content preparation, employee training, communications, and ongoing support. The project should also reserve funding for model usage growth, accessibility improvements, monitoring, periodic testing, and the addition of high-value integrations after the initial release.

A formal governance structure will oversee the program. The governing group will include representatives from technology, information security, privacy, legal, compliance, records management, human resources, and business leadership. It will approve the initial scope, review higher-risk use cases, monitor incidents and performance, and ensure that the assistant remains aligned with organizational policy and applicable law.

## Security, Privacy, and Responsible Use

Security and responsible use will be built into the deployment rather than added after launch. Employees will authenticate through the organization’s existing identity provider, and the assistant will enforce source-system permissions wherever content is retrieved. Sensitive information will be classified and handled according to existing policies. Data will be encrypted in transit and at rest, and administrative activity and significant user interactions will be logged for monitoring and investigation, subject to applicable privacy and records requirements.

The assistant will provide citations or links to source material whenever it answers questions from internal content. It will clearly indicate when it cannot verify an answer, and employees will be instructed to validate important outputs before relying on them. The platform will be tested for hallucinations, unauthorized data exposure, prompt injection, malicious content, biased or unsafe outputs, and inappropriate handling of personal or confidential information.

Employees will receive practical guidance on what information may be entered, how outputs may be used, when human review is mandatory, and how to report incorrect or harmful responses. The organization will maintain an incident process for investigating security events, privacy concerns, inaccurate content, and misuse. Access to higher-risk features will be restricted until the relevant controls and approval processes are in place.

## Success Criteria

The deployment will be considered successful when it demonstrates measurable employee value without compromising security, privacy, or trust. Within six months of organization-wide rollout, the target is for at least 70 percent of employees to have activated the assistant and at least 50 percent to use it monthly. At least 30 percent of employees should use it weekly for an approved work-related task, with adoption measured across departments rather than concentrated in a small group of early adopters.

For the initial priority use cases, the program should demonstrate a 20 percent or greater reduction in time spent on selected information-retrieval, drafting, and summarization tasks, based on baseline and post-deployment measurements. User surveys should show that at least 75 percent of active users consider the assistant useful for their work, and at least 70 percent should report improved ability to locate or understand internal information.

Quality and trust measures will be equally important. At least 90 percent of evaluated answers to approved knowledge questions should be factually correct, relevant, and supported by an authoritative source. Access-control testing should show no material instances of unauthorized information disclosure. All high-severity security, privacy, or safety issues must be investigated and resolved before broader release, and no unresolved critical issue may remain at the point of full deployment.

Operationally, the service should meet agreed availability and response-time targets, maintain a documented support process, and provide usage and quality reporting to the governance group. The organization should also demonstrate that employees have completed required training, that high-risk use cases are subject to documented review, and that content owners are maintaining the sources used by the assistant.

## Conclusion

A governed internal AI assistant can provide immediate value across a 5,000-employee organization by improving access to knowledge, reducing repetitive work, and establishing a consistent foundation for responsible enterprise AI adoption. A phased approach will allow the organization to demonstrate benefits quickly while managing the risks associated with inaccurate outputs, sensitive data, uneven content quality, and uncontrolled automation.

Approval of this proposal will authorize the discovery and design phase, appointment of the executive sponsor and product owner, formation of the cross-functional governance group, and development of a detailed implementation plan and budget. Subject to successful pilot results and satisfaction of the stated security, quality, and adoption criteria, the organization-wide assistant will become a supported enterprise service with a continuing roadmap for additional integrations and use cases.

The program will require an executive sponsor with authority across technology, business operations, risk, and people functions. A product owner will be accountable for the employee experience, use-case prioritization, and value realization. A program manager will coordinate delivery, governance, communications, dependencies, and reporting.

The core delivery team should include an AI or enterprise architect, two to three platform and integration engineers, two to three data and knowledge engineers, a security engineer, a privacy and risk specialist, a user-experience or service-design lead, a change-management and communications lead, a training lead, and a support or operations lead. The core team is expected to comprise approximately 12–16 dedicated full-time equivalent roles during implementation.

The program will also require part-time participation from representatives of Legal, Compliance, Information Security, Records Management, HR, IT Service Management, Communications, Accessibility, and major business functions. Approximately 20–30 subject-matter experts and departmental AI champions should participate in content validation, pilot testing, training, and adoption activities.

The organization should establish a first-year planning budget of approximately $1.5–$2.5 million, subject to the selected platform, licensing model, integration complexity, security requirements, and internal labor costs. This estimate includes implementation, configuration, content preparation, integration, training, change management, evaluation, and contingency. Ongoing operating costs are expected to be approximately $800,000–$1.5 million annually, including platform licensing, model usage, support, monitoring, security reviews, content stewardship, and continuous improvement. Final funding should be approved through a business case updated after the discovery and vendor-assessment phases.

The assistant should operate under a formal governance model. An AI Steering Committee should oversee policy, risk acceptance, investment, and expansion decisions. An operational AI Product Council should manage content quality, use-case approval, model performance, incident response, and changes to the assistant. Every connected knowledge source should have a business owner responsible for accuracy, review frequency, classification, and retirement of obsolete material.

## Security, Privacy, and Responsible Use

Security and privacy will be designed into the solution from the beginning. The assistant will use single sign-on, role-based access controls, encryption in transit and at rest, environment separation, audit logging, data-loss prevention, and continuous monitoring. Prompts and responses will be handled according to the organization’s information-classification requirements. Where a third-party model or platform is used, contracts must prohibit the use of organizational data for vendor model training unless explicitly approved.

The assistant will identify the sources supporting its answers whenever possible and will communicate uncertainty rather than present unsupported conclusions as fact. Employees will be informed that AI-generated outputs may contain errors and must be reviewed before being used in consequential decisions or external communications. A clear process will be established for reporting inaccurate, inappropriate, biased, or potentially sensitive responses.

Training will cover acceptable use, confidential information, personal data, intellectual property, human review, records obligations, and prohibited activities. The organization will also publish practical guidance explaining which tasks are suitable for the assistant and which require specialist review.

## Success Criteria

The project will be considered successful when the assistant is available to all employees through a reliable and secure service, with at least 70 percent of employees using it monthly and at least 40 percent using it weekly within six months of full rollout. At least 80 percent of active users should report that the assistant helps them complete work faster or access information more easily.

Quality testing and user feedback should demonstrate that at least 85 percent of sampled responses are useful, relevant, and appropriately supported by approved sources. The program should achieve a 20–25 percent reduction in time required to locate common internal information and a 15–20 percent reduction in repetitive inquiries to participating IT, HR, and other support functions. Pilot groups should demonstrate measurable time savings in at least three priority use cases, such as policy navigation, document summarization, meeting follow-up, or service-desk support.

Operationally, the service should meet an availability target of at least 99.5 percent during business hours, maintain defined response-time standards, and complete scheduled security, privacy, and access-control reviews. There should be no unresolved critical privacy or security incidents attributable to the assistant, and all high-risk use cases should remain subject to documented human oversight.

Employee trust will be measured through recurring surveys, feedback trends, incident reports, and usage patterns. Success will not be defined solely by adoption; it will depend on sustained usage, demonstrable business value, responsible behavior, and confidence that the assistant provides secure access to reliable organizational knowledge.

## Recommendation

The organization should approve the twelve-month phased program and authorize the discovery and design phase immediately. Beginning with a controlled pilot will allow the organization to demonstrate value, identify risks, improve content quality, and establish governance before extending access to the full workforce. With appropriate investment and oversight, an internal AI assistant can become a practical enterprise service that improves day-to-day productivity while creating a responsible foundation for broader AI-enabled transformation.

# Proposal: Deployment of an Internal AI Assistant Across the Organization

## Background

The organization’s 5,000 employees rely on a growing volume of policies, procedures, reports, project documents, knowledge bases, and business applications to perform their work. Although this information is valuable, it is often distributed across multiple systems, difficult to search, and inconsistently maintained. Employees spend significant time locating information, drafting routine communications, summarizing documents, preparing meeting materials, and requesting assistance from subject-matter experts.

Recent advances in generative artificial intelligence provide an opportunity to improve access to organizational knowledge and reduce time spent on repetitive knowledge work. An internal AI assistant can provide employees with a secure, conversational interface for finding approved information, creating first drafts, summarizing content, and completing selected low-risk tasks. Deployed responsibly, the assistant can improve productivity while preserving human accountability, data governance, and existing approval processes.

This proposal recommends a phased deployment of an enterprise AI assistant for all employees, beginning with a controlled pilot and expanding after security, quality, adoption, and operational criteria have been met. The assistant will be designed as an enterprise service rather than an isolated chatbot, with integration into approved information sources, identity systems, collaboration tools, and selected business workflows.

## Objectives

The primary objective is to give every employee secure, reliable, and practical access to AI assistance within the flow of daily work. The service will help employees locate information, understand complex material, create and revise content, and perform routine knowledge tasks more efficiently.

The initiative will pursue five specific objectives. First, it will improve information access by allowing employees to ask questions in natural language and receive answers grounded in approved internal content, with links to source material wherever possible. Second, it will increase productivity by supporting drafting, summarization, analysis, translation, meeting preparation, and other repetitive tasks. Third, it will improve consistency by directing employees to current policies, standard processes, templates, and approved guidance. Fourth, it will establish a secure and governed foundation for future AI-enabled workflows. Finally, it will develop employee capability and confidence through training, clear usage guidance, and transparent communication about the technology’s benefits and limitations.

The assistant will augment employees rather than replace professional judgment. It will provide recommendations and draft outputs, but employees will remain responsible for reviewing content and making decisions. The system will not be positioned as an authoritative source for legal, medical, financial, employment, safety, or other high-impact decisions without appropriate human review.

## Scope

The first release will provide a secure conversational assistant accessible through the organization’s existing collaboration environment and web applications. Employees will authenticate through the organization’s identity provider, and access to information will follow existing role-based permissions. The assistant will not expose documents or data to a user who could not already access them through the source system.

Initial capabilities will include enterprise search and question answering over approved internal content; summarization of documents, email threads, and meeting materials; drafting and editing of routine communications; creation of outlines, briefs, reports, and presentations; extraction of action items and decisions; translation and plain-language rewriting; and assistance with approved policies, procedures, and templates. Where appropriate, responses will include citations or links to source documents and will clearly indicate when the assistant is uncertain or lacks sufficient information.

The service will initially connect to selected, high-value repositories such as the intranet, policy library, document management platform, knowledge base, and collaboration tools. Additional integrations may include customer relationship management, service management, human resources, finance, or project systems, provided that the use case has a defined business owner, appropriate data classification, and an approved control model.

The initial scope will not include unrestricted access to confidential or regulated information, fully autonomous execution of business transactions, automated employment or personnel decisions, external customer communications without review, or any workflow that can create material legal, financial, operational, or reputational consequences without human authorization. These capabilities may be considered in later phases following separate risk assessment and approval.

A formal governance framework will accompany the technology. It will define acceptable use, prohibited uses, data-handling requirements, records-management responsibilities, escalation procedures, model evaluation standards, and accountability for connected data sources. The organization will also establish a process for reporting inaccurate, harmful, biased, or inappropriate responses and for rapidly removing problematic content or integrations.

## Delivery Approach and Timeline

The program is expected to run for approximately twelve months from approval to organization-wide adoption, followed by continuous improvement.

During the first two months, the program team will establish governance, confirm business priorities, assess the current technology and data landscape, and select the technical platform. This phase will include privacy, security, legal, procurement, records-management, accessibility, and labor-relations reviews where applicable. The team will identify the initial information sources, define data classifications, document use-case requirements, and establish baseline measures for productivity, employee experience, service-desk volume, and information retrieval.

During months three and four, the organization will build the minimum viable service. This work will include identity and access integration, model and platform configuration, retrieval of approved enterprise content, logging and monitoring, content filtering, administrative controls, and user-experience design. The team will create an initial set of tested use cases and establish evaluation procedures covering factual accuracy, source attribution, security, privacy, bias, prompt injection, resilience, and performance. A small group of representative employees from business, operational, technical, and corporate functions will participate in usability testing.

During months five and six, the assistant will enter a controlled pilot involving approximately 250 to 500 employees across a representative set of departments. Pilot participants will receive training on effective prompting, verification of AI-generated content, confidential-data handling, and appropriate use of the service. Feedback will be collected through surveys, interviews, usage analytics, quality reviews, and support tickets. The team will refine retrieval settings, improve source content, address usability issues, and confirm that operational support and incident-response processes are ready for broader use.

During months seven and eight, the service will expand to approximately 1,500 employees, including managers, knowledge workers, frontline support teams, and departments with high volumes of routine documentation and information requests. Additional approved content sources will be connected, and selected low-risk workflow integrations may be introduced. The organization will assess adoption, answer quality, employee time savings, system performance, and control effectiveness. Expansion will proceed only if the service meets agreed quality and security thresholds.

During months nine and ten, the assistant will be made available to the remaining employees in managed waves. Each wave will be supported by communications, short-form training, departmental champions, and clearly identified help channels. Usage guidance will be incorporated into onboarding and relevant professional-development programs. Departments will be encouraged to identify local use cases, but all new data sources and automated actions will remain subject to central governance.

During months eleven and twelve, the program will transition from deployment to steady-state operations. The team will complete a formal benefits review, resolve outstanding issues, document operating procedures, and present a recommendation for the next phase. The next phase may include additional enterprise data sources, specialized assistants for approved functions, workflow automation, and more advanced analytics, subject to demonstrated value and risk controls.

## Resource Requirements

The initiative will require executive sponsorship, a clear product owner, and a cross-functional delivery team. The recommended core team consists of an executive sponsor, program or product manager, enterprise architect, AI or machine-learning engineers, data and integration engineers, information-security specialists, privacy and legal representatives, user-experience and service-design staff, content and knowledge-management leads, change-management and communications personnel, quality-assurance analysts, and service-support representatives.

During the build and pilot phases, the organization should plan for approximately 12 to 18 dedicated full-time-equivalent staff, supplemented by part-time subject-matter experts and departmental champions. After organization-wide deployment, the ongoing operating model will likely require approximately 8 to 12 full-time-equivalent staff across product management, platform operations, security and governance, data curation, user support, training, and continuous improvement. Business units will also need designated content owners who are accountable for the accuracy, currency, and access permissions of information made available to the assistant.

The technology environment will require an approved large-language-model platform, secure application hosting, identity and access management, document and data connectors, vector or semantic search capabilities, monitoring and analytics, data-loss-prevention controls, audit logging, and service-management integration. The selected platform should support enterprise data isolation, configurable retention, encryption in transit and at rest, administrative controls, model-performance monitoring, and contractual commitments appropriate to the organization’s data requirements. The design should avoid using employee prompts or organizational data to train public models unless explicitly approved.

A preliminary first-year budget of approximately $1.5 million to $2.5 million is recommended, subject to the chosen platform, licensing model, integration complexity, security requirements, and internal staffing costs. This estimate includes implementation, software or model usage, integration, security and testing, training, communications, support, and contingency. A detailed business case should be completed during the first phase using expected usage volumes and the organization’s data and compliance requirements.

## Governance, Risk, and Change Management

The assistant will operate under an AI governance committee chaired by an executive sponsor and including representatives from technology, security, privacy, legal, risk, human resources, records management, accessibility, and business operations. The committee will approve use cases, determine risk classifications, review performance, and authorize new integrations or autonomous capabilities.

The system will enforce existing permissions, restrict access to approved data, and maintain auditable records of administrative activity and system performance. Prompts and responses will be handled according to defined retention and privacy policies. Sensitive information will be protected through data classification, filtering, access controls, and monitoring. The organization will conduct regular testing for inaccurate answers, unsafe recommendations, discriminatory outputs, unauthorized data exposure, prompt injection, and other emerging risks.

Adoption will be supported through practical training rather than a one-time announcement. Employees will learn how to use the assistant effectively, verify its output, protect confidential information, recognize hallucinations or unsupported claims, and escalate problems. Departmental champions will help identify valuable use cases and reinforce responsible practices. Communications will emphasize that the assistant is a governed productivity tool, not an infallible source of truth or a substitute for professional accountability.

## Success Criteria

The deployment will be considered successful when the assistant is available to all employees through approved channels, operates within defined security and privacy controls, and demonstrates measurable value in everyday work.

Within six months of organization-wide availability, the program should achieve a target of at least 60 percent monthly active usage among eligible employees, with at least 40 percent using the assistant weekly. At least 75 percent of surveyed users should report that it saves time or improves the quality of their work, and at least 70 percent should rate the service as easy to use. The organization should identify measurable time savings in priority use cases, such as document summarization, information retrieval, drafting, meeting preparation, and policy interpretation.

For quality, at least 90 percent of evaluated responses in approved enterprise question-answering use cases should be materially accurate and appropriately grounded in cited source content. Responses that require human review should be clearly identified, and critical incidents involving unauthorized data disclosure should remain at zero. Security, privacy, accessibility, and availability targets will be established before the pilot and monitored continuously thereafter.

The program should also demonstrate operational sustainability. Support volumes should stabilize after rollout, content owners should meet defined freshness standards, and the organization should maintain a documented process for evaluating new use cases and retiring low-value or unsafe ones. At the end of the first year, the executive steering group will review adoption, employee productivity, user satisfaction, risk performance, operating cost, and realized business benefits. Continued investment and expansion will be based on this evidence rather than usage alone.

## Recommendation

The organization should approve a phased, governed deployment of an internal AI assistant beginning with a two-month foundation phase and progressing through pilot, controlled expansion, and organization-wide rollout over twelve months. This approach will provide employees with immediate practical assistance while giving the organization time to validate value, improve data quality, manage risk, and establish sustainable operating practices. With appropriate investment and oversight, the assistant can become a secure enterprise capability that improves access to knowledge, reduces repetitive work, and creates a foundation for responsible AI-enabled services across the organization.

A department will have three people on parental leave, one contractor whose contract was quietly extended, and a regional office that cannot accept shipments without a week’s notice. Someone will be running a line-of-business application that only works on an older operating system, while someone else has managed to make their entire workflow depend on a browser extension nobody has documented. None of these cases is difficult in isolation. Together, they turn a replacement program into a long series of small negotiations, each one capable of delaying the schedule just enough to make the schedule meaningless.

The real work is keeping the exceptions visible without letting them become the plan. That means maintaining an inventory people can trust, assigning ownership for every unreturned device, and deciding in advance what happens when a user misses their appointment or refuses the standard configuration. It also means treating data migration, access checks, shipping, disposal, and communications as part of the refresh rather than administrative weather around it. A successful cycle is not the one where every box arrives on time. It is the one where, six months later, nobody can remember which problems were caused by the refresh and which were merely waiting for an excuse.

A site will have one machine that runs a control system nobody documented, another whose warranty depends on a vendor portal tied to a former employee, and a third that technically meets the specification but cannot fit through the only door wide enough to reach the rack. The inventory will be accurate in the way old maps are accurate: useful for orientation, unreliable at the point of contact. Every exception creates a small decision, and every small decision quietly becomes a dependency.

By the time the replacement units arrive, the project is no longer about replacing equipment. It is about sequencing downtime, preserving institutional memory, finding compatible parts, and persuading six different teams that their edge case is not an argument for keeping the old fleet forever. The successful refresh is the one that treats those details as part of the asset, not as noise around it.

A site needs a different keyboard layout. A manager wants to keep a machine that was scheduled for retirement because it contains one application nobody has documented. Someone is on extended leave, someone else has just joined, and the replacement units are now sitting in a warehouse while the service desk tries to determine which address is still current. None of these issues is difficult in isolation. Together, they turn a clean rollout into a sequence of small negotiations.

The real work is keeping those negotiations from becoming the operating model. You need a decision log that people will actually update, an owner for every unresolved exception, and a cutoff date that is treated as a cutoff rather than an invitation to submit better arguments. The final inventory will not match the first one, and that is not a failure. The failure is discovering six months later that the differences were never recorded, so the next refresh begins with the same assumptions and a fresh spreadsheet.

A regional office will need machines with a port that disappeared three product generations ago. Someone will discover that the warehouse still depends on a line-of-business application certified only for an operating system nobody wants to support. A vice president will ask whether the new devices can be made to look exactly like the old ones, preferably without changing any settings, habits, or expectations.

By the time the first shipment arrives, the refresh has stopped being a replacement project and become a small exercise in institutional archaeology. You are no longer deciding what to buy; you are reconstructing why twelve different people made twelve different compromises over the last seven years. The successful rollout is the one that leaves the fewest of those compromises visible, which is less satisfying than a clean deployment plan but considerably closer to the truth.

# Project Proposal: Enterprise Internal AI Assistant

## Background

This proposal recommends the design, implementation, and organization-wide deployment of a secure internal AI assistant for a 5,000-employee organization. The assistant will give employees a conversational way to find trusted internal information, summarize documents, draft routine communications, navigate policies and procedures, and receive guidance on common IT, HR, operations, and business-process questions.

Employees currently spend significant time searching across document repositories, intranets, collaboration platforms, email, and service portals. Valuable knowledge is often difficult to locate, inconsistently maintained, or dependent on individual subject-matter experts. An internal AI assistant can reduce this friction and improve access to institutional knowledge, but an unmanaged solution could create unacceptable risks, including disclosure of confidential information, inaccurate answers, unapproved use of sensitive data, and overreliance on automated recommendations.

The proposed solution will therefore be deployed as a governed enterprise service rather than as an open-ended chatbot. It will use an approved AI platform, enterprise identity controls, permission-aware retrieval, source citations, audit logging, content ownership, and clear human-accountability requirements. The assistant will initially focus on low- and medium-risk use cases and will not make autonomous decisions or modify business records without explicit approval.

## Objectives

The primary objective is to provide employees with fast, reliable access to approved organizational knowledge through a secure conversational interface. The assistant will allow users to ask questions in natural language and receive responses grounded in approved sources, with links or citations that allow the user to verify the information.

The project will also improve productivity by reducing the time employees spend locating policies, procedures, templates, and technical guidance; accelerate the preparation of routine drafts and summaries; and reduce repetitive inquiries handled by HR, IT, operations, and other support teams. It will establish a repeatable governance and operating model for future AI capabilities, including risk assessment, data stewardship, model evaluation, user training, incident management, and continuous improvement.

The program will measure its impact against defined business baselines rather than relying solely on usage statistics. Success will be determined by whether the assistant is trusted, useful, secure, adopted across the organization, and capable of producing measurable time savings without creating material operational or compliance risk.

## Scope

The first release will provide an employee-facing assistant accessible through a secure web interface and, where appropriate, an approved collaboration platform such as Microsoft Teams or Slack. Employees will authenticate through the organization’s existing single sign-on service. Access to information will inherit the permissions of the underlying systems, ensuring that the assistant cannot expose content a user could not access directly.

The initial knowledge base will include approved policies, procedures, employee guidance, IT documentation, service information, operational manuals, frequently asked questions, templates, and selected business-process documentation. Priority use cases will include answering policy and process questions, supporting employee onboarding, providing IT self-service guidance, summarizing approved documents, helping users locate forms and templates, and drafting routine internal communications. Each response will identify its supporting sources whenever the use case permits.

The project will include data-source assessment and preparation, identity and access integration, content connectors, search and retrieval configuration, prompt and response guardrails, monitoring, analytics, user feedback, security testing, privacy assessment, accessibility review, employee training, communications, service-desk preparation, and post-launch support. Content owners will be assigned for each major knowledge domain and will be responsible for accuracy, currency, and retention of the material provided to the assistant.

The first release will not include public or customer-facing access, unrestricted ingestion of confidential or regulated information, autonomous employment or financial decisions, legal or medical advice, or unsupervised actions that create, approve, delete, or change business records. Write-back capabilities and workflow automation may be considered in a later phase, but only after separate security, privacy, legal, and operational reviews. The assistant will supplement existing systems of record and will not replace authoritative HR, finance, IT service-management, document-management, or compliance platforms.

## Governance and Delivery Approach

An executive sponsor, preferably the CIO, COO, or equivalent, will provide accountability and remove organizational barriers. An AI Steering Committee will oversee the program and include representatives from information security, privacy, legal, risk, HR, IT, records management, accessibility, communications, and major business functions.

Before any source is connected, the project team will classify the data, confirm its owner, validate access controls, determine retention requirements, and document approved use cases. The selected platform and model provider must meet organizational requirements for encryption, data residency, retention, auditability, availability, and contractual restrictions on using organizational prompts and content for provider model training unless explicitly approved.

The assistant will be designed to acknowledge uncertainty, cite sources, decline unsupported requests, and direct users to a human or authoritative system when a question is outside its approved scope. Production activity will be logged in accordance with privacy and employment requirements. The organization will maintain procedures for reporting incorrect answers, suspected data exposure, harmful outputs, service interruptions, and policy violations. A formal review will take place before each expansion of the assistant’s data access or action capabilities.

## Timeline

The implementation will be completed in approximately ten months following project approval, assuming timely participation from business and technical stakeholders.

During the first month, the project will establish the charter, executive sponsorship, governance structure, business case, risk assessment, and success baselines. The team will identify and prioritize use cases, inventory potential data sources, assess content quality, confirm regulatory and privacy requirements, and select or validate the enterprise AI platform. A representative evaluation set of real organizational questions will be created so that the assistant can be tested consistently throughout the project.

During months two and three, the team will build the technical foundation. This work will include configuring the approved AI environment, integrating single sign-on, implementing role-based access, connecting the first knowledge sources, establishing logging and monitoring, defining response policies, and creating the initial user experience. Security testing, privacy review, accessibility testing, and content validation will be conducted before the first pilot. A controlled technical pilot of approximately 150 users will be used to identify defects and improve the assistant’s grounding and usability.

During months four and five, the assistant will enter a broader controlled pilot of approximately 500 employees representing IT, HR, operations, and selected business functions. The pilot will test priority use cases, source quality, response accuracy, adoption barriers, support processes, and training materials. Red-team testing will evaluate prompt injection, unauthorized retrieval, sensitive-data exposure, inaccurate guidance, and attempts to bypass safeguards. The Steering Committee will make a formal decision at the end of this phase on whether the service is ready for scaled deployment.

During months six and seven, the assistant will be rolled out in the first enterprise wave to approximately 2,000 employees. Deployment will be supported by role-based training, manager communications, office hours, in-product guidance, and service-desk support. Usage, feedback, response quality, and security telemetry will be reviewed weekly, with adjustments made before the next wave.

During months eight and nine, the remaining approximately 2,500 employees will be onboarded. Additional approved content sources may be added, subject to the same governance and testing requirements. The project will also finalize the support model, content stewardship responsibilities, incident procedures, and product roadmap.

Month ten will be dedicated to stabilization, benefits measurement, remediation of outstanding issues, and transition from project delivery to ongoing service operations. The final review will document performance against the success criteria and recommend whether to expand use cases, add workflow actions, or adjust the operating model.

## Resource Requirements

The project will require a core delivery team of approximately 12 to 15 full-time-equivalent staff during implementation. This team will include an executive sponsor, program manager, product owner, enterprise architect, AI or machine-learning engineers, data and integration engineers, a security architect, privacy and risk representatives, a user-experience or service designer, a quality and evaluation lead, a change-management and training lead, and a service-operations representative. The organization should also provide 20 to 30 part-time subject-matter experts and content owners from participating departments to validate use cases, prepare source material, evaluate responses, and support adoption.

The technical environment will require an enterprise AI platform or approved model service, secure search and retrieval capabilities, document connectors, identity and access integration, application monitoring, security-information and event-management integration, data-loss-prevention controls, evaluation tooling, and appropriate development, test, and production environments. Existing enterprise licenses and platforms should be used wherever practical to reduce duplication and simplify support.

A preliminary first-year funding envelope of approximately $1.5 million to $3 million should be reserved for platform licensing and model usage, implementation services, integration, security and privacy testing, content preparation, training, communications, support, and contingency. The final amount will depend on whether the organization extends an existing platform or procures a new service, the volume and sensitivity of connected content, expected usage, and the number of integrations required. After launch, a steady-state operating team of approximately four to six full-time-equivalent staff, supplemented by departmental content stewards, should maintain the service, monitor performance, manage incidents, evaluate new use cases, and oversee platform and model changes.

## Success Criteria

The project will be considered successful when the assistant is demonstrably useful, secure, and sustainable at enterprise scale. Within six months of full deployment, at least 70 percent of employees should have activated the service, at least 60 percent should be monthly active users, and user surveys should show an average usefulness rating of at least 4.0 out of 5. At least 80 percent of pilot and early-release users should complete required training or in-product guidance.

On a representative benchmark of organizational questions, at least 90 percent of responses should be judged accurate and adequately grounded in approved sources, with valid citations provided for supported knowledge queries. The service should maintain at least 99.5 percent availability during the stabilization period, meet agreed response-time targets, and provide complete audit records for production activity.

The organization should achieve a measured reduction of at least 15 percent in the time required to locate common policies, procedures, and operational guidance, along with a 10 percent reduction in repetitive eligible IT, HR, or operations inquiries. These measures will be validated through pre-launch baselines, user surveys, service-desk data, task-time studies, and controlled comparisons where feasible.

Security and governance requirements are mandatory success criteria. All connected sources must have documented owners and permission-aware access controls. The service must pass security, privacy, accessibility, and compliance reviews; demonstrate that unauthorized retrieval is blocked; and operate without any material data-exposure incident during the pilot or rollout. High-risk questions must be declined or routed to an appropriate human or authoritative system. The service must also have an approved post-launch owner, funding model, support process, content-maintenance schedule, and quarterly performance and risk-review cycle.

Approval of this proposal will authorize the organization to begin the first month of discovery and mobilization. The program will deliver a controlled, measurable, and secure foundation for internal AI use while creating a practical path toward broader automation and knowledge-management improvements.

# Project Proposal: Enterprise Internal AI Assistant

## Background

Employees currently spend significant time searching for information, interpreting internal policies, drafting routine communications, summarizing meetings and documents, and navigating multiple business systems. Knowledge is distributed across document repositories, collaboration platforms, intranets, service desks and line-of-business applications, making it difficult to find accurate, current information quickly. At the same time, employees are increasingly using public AI tools independently, creating potential risks related to confidentiality, data retention, intellectual property and inconsistent outputs.

This proposal recommends deploying a secure, centrally governed AI assistant for the organization’s 5,000 employees. The assistant will provide conversational access to approved internal knowledge and support common productivity tasks while respecting existing identity, access and data-classification controls. It will be designed as an augmentation tool rather than a replacement for employee judgment, official systems or subject-matter expertise.

## Objectives

The primary objective is to improve employee productivity by reducing the time required to locate information, create first drafts, summarize content and complete routine knowledge-work tasks. The assistant will help employees obtain reliable answers from approved internal sources, with citations or links back to the underlying content wherever possible.

A second objective is to establish a safe and consistent enterprise standard for using generative AI. The solution will provide a controlled alternative to unsanctioned public tools and will incorporate single sign-on, role-based access, data-loss prevention, audit logging, retention controls and clear rules for acceptable use. The assistant must never give a user access to information that the user could not already access through the source system.

The program will also create a scalable foundation for future AI-enabled workflows. Once the core platform, governance model and operating processes are established, the organization can evaluate more specialized applications in functions such as customer support, finance, human resources, legal, operations and technology.

## Scope

The first release will provide a web-based assistant integrated with the organization’s existing identity and collaboration environment. Subject to technical and security review, it will connect to approved document repositories, knowledge bases, intranet content, service-management systems and selected business applications. Access to content will be permission-aware, and responses will identify the sources used to generate them.

Initial use cases will include searching and answering questions about internal policies and procedures; summarizing documents, meetings and email threads; drafting and rewriting routine business content; extracting action items and decisions; preparing briefing materials; and helping employees navigate internal services. Selected teams may also use the assistant for read-only retrieval of operational information, provided the underlying data is approved for that purpose.

The program will include a pilot, user training, communications, administrator capabilities, usage analytics, content-quality processes, security testing and ongoing support. It will also establish an AI usage policy, an intake process for new use cases, an incident-management procedure and an evaluation framework for accuracy, usefulness, bias, privacy and security.

The initial scope will not include fully autonomous actions, unrestricted access to confidential data, unsupervised external communications, or decisions affecting employment, legal matters, financial approvals, health, safety or regulatory compliance. The assistant will not replace official records, policies or systems of record. Any future workflow automation will require a separate risk assessment, business case and approval.

## Delivery Approach and Timeline

The deployment will follow a phased, twelve-month approach designed to demonstrate value early while allowing time for appropriate governance and testing.

During months one and two, the program will be mobilized. An executive sponsor and cross-functional steering committee will be appointed, target use cases will be prioritized, and existing data sources will be inventoried and classified. The team will establish requirements for identity, access control, privacy, security, retention, model hosting and integration. A baseline will also be created for current search time, productivity measures, help-desk demand and employee sentiment so that benefits can be measured consistently.

During months three and four, the organization will select or confirm the technology platform and build a controlled sandbox. The team will configure single sign-on, role-based access, audit logging and administrative controls; connect a limited number of approved knowledge sources; and establish content-indexing and permission-synchronization processes. Sample questions and representative documents will be used to test response quality, source attribution, prompt-injection resistance, data leakage and inappropriate content generation.

During months five and six, the assistant will be piloted with approximately 300 to 500 employees representing different functions, roles and levels of technical familiarity. Pilot users will receive role-based training and clear guidance on appropriate use. Their feedback, usage patterns and reported issues will be reviewed weekly. The pilot will measure answer quality, time saved, user confidence, adoption, support demand and any security or privacy concerns. A formal go/no-go review will determine whether the platform is ready for broader deployment.

During months seven and eight, the program will incorporate pilot findings, improve the user experience, expand approved content sources and finalize the production operating model. Governance policies, service-level targets, support procedures and escalation paths will be confirmed. Additional testing will be completed with security, privacy, legal and compliance stakeholders.

During months nine through eleven, deployment will proceed in controlled waves of approximately 1,000 to 1,500 employees. Each wave will include communications, training, manager enablement and access to support. The rollout will prioritize functions with strong knowledge-management needs and suitable data readiness. Usage and performance will be reviewed after each wave before the next group is enabled.

During month twelve, the program will transition from implementation to steady-state operations. The organization will complete a benefits review, address remaining adoption barriers, confirm the roadmap for additional integrations and establish a quarterly process for evaluating new use cases. The platform will then be managed as an enterprise service with ongoing governance, monitoring and improvement.

## Resource Requirements

The implementation will require an estimated 12 to 16 dedicated full-time equivalent resources during the first year, supplemented by part-time subject-matter experts and business data owners. The core team will include an executive sponsor, program manager, product owner, enterprise architect, integration and platform engineers, data and search specialists, security and privacy representatives, legal or compliance support, user-experience and change-management leads, training resources and service-desk personnel.

Business units participating in the pilot will provide subject-matter experts to validate content, define priority use cases and assess response quality. Each connected data source will require an accountable owner responsible for data accuracy, access permissions and retention requirements. After rollout, the operating model will require a smaller permanent team to manage the product roadmap, platform administration, content quality, analytics, support, vendor relationships and governance.

Technology funding will cover enterprise AI platform or model licensing for up to 5,000 employees, secure hosting, storage and search infrastructure, integration development, monitoring, security testing, training materials and implementation support. The selected platform must provide enterprise data protections, contractual restrictions on using organizational content to train shared models, configurable retention, administrative reporting and reliable integration with the organization’s existing identity and security tools. A contingency should be included for additional connectors, data remediation and adoption support.

The program will be governed by a steering committee representing technology, information security, privacy, legal, human resources, risk, communications and major business functions. A formal AI policy will define permitted and prohibited uses, employee responsibilities, handling of sensitive information, human-review requirements and procedures for reporting incorrect or harmful outputs. All production use cases will be evaluated according to risk, and higher-risk applications will require additional approval.

## Success Criteria

The deployment will be considered successful when it delivers measurable productivity benefits without compromising information security, privacy or trust. Within six months of full rollout, the target is for at least 60 percent of employees to use the assistant monthly and at least 35 percent to use it weekly. At least 95 percent of enabled employees should complete required training, and at least 80 percent of surveyed users should rate the assistant as useful for one or more regular work activities.

For the initial use cases, the organization should achieve a measured reduction of at least 20 percent in time spent on information search, document summarization and routine drafting, compared with the baseline established during discovery. At least 85 percent of sampled responses should meet the agreed standards for relevance, factual grounding and appropriate source attribution. Each participating business function should identify at least one repeatable use case with a documented productivity or service improvement.

Operationally, the service should achieve at least 99.5 percent availability during business hours and meet agreed response-time targets. All production interactions must be subject to the organization’s access controls and audit requirements. The program must have no high-severity data-loss or privacy incidents, and all identified critical vulnerabilities must be addressed before production release. Employee feedback, support trends and evaluation results will be reviewed quarterly to ensure that quality and trust remain stable as adoption grows.

The expected result is a secure, measurable and sustainable enterprise capability that helps employees work more effectively today while giving the organization a controlled foundation for broader AI-enabled services in the future.

These standards will support future AI-enabled applications without requiring the organization to build governance from the beginning for each new initiative.
